Text: The novel opens with the family in the hold of a sailing ship, weathering a great storm. The ship runs aground on a reef, and the family learns the ship's crew has taken to a lifeboat and abandoned them. Subsequent searches for the crew yield no trace. The ship survives the night as the storm abates, and the family finds themselves within sight of a tropical island. The ship's cargo of livestock, dogs, guns & powder, carpentry tools, books, a disassembled pinnace, and provisions have survived. The family builds a raft, lashes livestock and the most valuable supplies to it, and paddles to the island, where they set up a temporary shelter. Over the next few weeks they make several expeditions back to the ship, to empty its hold, and harvest rigging, planks, and sails. They construct a small homestead on the island, and the ship's hull eventually breaks up in a storm and founders. The middle of the book is a series of vignettes, covering several years. The father and older boys explore various environments about the island, discover various (improbable) plants and animals, and build a large tree house, complete with a library. They also use the carpentry tools and local resources to build mechanical contraptions. Eventually, sailing the pinnace around the island's coast, they discover a European family hiding from local pirates. They adopt their daughter (who at first masquerades as a boy), and her father returns on a rescue mission, restoring the family's contact to the outside world.

Laura Chant has one of her "warnings", a premonition that something is about to happen, but is forced to ignore it and go to school as usual. On the way home, she and her younger brother Jacko encounter the sinister Carmody Braque, who 'playfully' stamps Jacko's hand, the stamp appearing as an image of his face. As Jacko becomes increasingly ill, Laura believes he has been possessed. She seeks the help of Sorensen "Sorry" Carlisle, recognized by her as a witch in hiding though to others he seems just a painfully well-behaved school prefect who photographs birds as a hobby. She learns that Braque is an ancient being who consumes the life force of others to keep himself alive. Sorry's grandmother Winter, one of a long line of witches, recommends that Laura should "changeover" from her normal life, becoming a witch or "woman of the moon" herself. As such she can trick the unwary Braque into putting himself in her power. Although warned that the changeover can be dangerous, Laura is determined to save her brother, now very near death. Laura experiences the changeover as a spirit journey through a dark forest, which is also at the same time Gardendale. The Carlisle witches help her through it, for their own reasons, and she emerges from the perilous passage with the power of nature and imagination awakened in her. Taking Sorensen along to mask her new power, Laura confronts Braque and succeeds in gaining power over him and breaking his hold on Jacko. At first intending to make the evil entity suffer, she rejects the dark temptation and instead ends his unnatural existence.

Jeremy Fisher is a frog who lives in a damp little house amongst the buttercups at the edge of a pond. His larder and back passage are "slippy-sloppy" with water, but he likes getting his feet wet; no one ever scolds and he never catches cold. One day, Jeremy finds it raining and decides to go fishing. Should he catch more than five minnows, he will invite his friends to dinner. He puts on a Macintosh and shiny goloshes, takes his rod and basket, and sets off with "enormous hops" to the place where he keeps his lily-pad boat. He poles to a place he knows is good for minnows. Once there, he sits cross-legged on his lily-pad and arranges his tackle. He has "the dearest little red float". His rod is a stalk of grass and his line a horsehair. An hour passes without a nibble. He takes a break and lunches on a butterfly sandwich. A water beetle tweaks his toe, and rats rustling about in the rushes force him to seek a safer location. He drops his line into the water and immediately has a bite. It is not a minnow but little Jack Sharp, a stickleback. The fish escapes but not before Jeremy pricks his fingers on Jack's spines. A shoal of little fishes come to the surface to laugh at Jeremy. Jeremy sucks his sore fingers, but a trout rises from the water and seizes him with a snap (Mr. Jeremy screams, "OW-OW-OW!!!"). The trout dives to the bottom, but finds the Macintosh tasteless and spits Jeremy out, swallowing only his goloshes. Jeremy bounces "up to the surface of the water, like a cork and the bubbles out of a soda water bottle", and swims to the pond's edge. He scrambles up the bank and hops home through the meadow, quite sure he will never go fishing again. In the last few pages, Jeremy has put sticking plaster on his fingers and welcomes his friends, Sir Isaac Newton, a newt, and Alderman Ptolemy Tortoise, a tortoise who eats salad. Isaac wears a black and gold waistcoat and Ptolemy brings a salad in a string bag. Jeremy has prepared roasted grasshopper with ladybird sauce. The narrator describes the dish as a "frog treat", but thinks "it must have been nasty!"

Artemis Fowl lures Mulch Diggums, a dwarf, to work with him to steal a tiara for a laser he is developing. A band of other dwarfs, using a circus as their cover have already stolen the tiara. The other dwarfs, led by Sergei the Significant, are planning to sell it to a jewellery fence. Captain Holly Short is on a break pending a tribunal after the Fowl Manor Incident, but Foaly tells her that the LEP have been alerted by Mulch Diggum's stolen helmet, about Artemis Fowl. Holly immediately heads to Ireland and confronts the dwarfs. Soon after Holly has tagged all of the dwarfs in Sergei's band, she chases Artemis and Mulch. Mulch and Artemis soon split with Artemis promising to write Mulch a cheque for the tiara. Holly chases after Artemis and demands the tiara and a LEP helmet from him. Artemis gives her the LEP helmet but keeps the tiara. Holly forces Artemis to give her the tiara, and then he hands it over. Later on we learn that Artemis switched the gemstone in the tiara with a fake one. He gives the real one to his mother because it reminds her of Artemis's father, specifically, the color of his eyes.

The Fafhrd and Gray Mouser stories follow the lives of two larcenous but likable rogues as they adventure across the fantasy world of Nehwon. The pieces in Swords Against Death follow the duo as they shake the dust of Lankhmar from their feet in the wake of the deaths their of their first loves, only to find their resolution never to return pointless ("The Circle Curse"). There follow a miscellaneous series of adventures from their wanderings, including a quest for treasure in a dwelling with unique defenses ("The Jewels in the Forest"), a return bout with the Thieves' Guild they hold responsible for their ladies' deaths ("Thieves' House"), an ensorcelled journey to a far-away land ("The Bleak Shore"), an encounter with a beast-haunted stranger ("The Howling Tower"), a dangerous visit to the Nehwonian equivalent of Atlantis ("The Sunken Land"), a conflict with a murderous priesthood ("The Seven Black Priests"), a magical plague afflicting Lankhmar ("Claws from the Night"), a final parting with their deceased loves in the Shadowland ("The Price of Pain-Ease"), and an investigation of a mysterious shop that is other than it seems ""Bazaar of the Bizarre").

Family Voices exposes the story of a mother, son, and dead husband and father through a series of letters that the mother and son have written to one another and that each speaks aloud. The son has moved off to the city and is surrounded by odd characters and circumstances. The mother, who apparently never receives her son's letters, questions angrily why her son never responds to her letters, and brings news of his father's death. Towards the end of the play, the father speaks as it were from the grave, "Just to keep in touch" (81). A series of interlocking monologues spoken by three Voices (One, Two, and Three), Family Voices exposes themes involving difficulties of communication, the vicissitudes of memory and the past, and family dysfunction familiar from Pinter's other dramatic works, employing some of Pinter's well-known stylistic traits. The peculiar circumstances of the characters evoke the Theatre of the Absurd. The mother and son continually have trouble communicating with each other, resulting in more intense attempts at communication that only serve to make the situation more absurd.

In a bid to uncover whether Babe Ruth pointed to his famed “called shot” during the 1932 World Series, Joe Stoshack travels back in time, accompanied by his father to ensure safety and to chase a paycheck since he’s been recently laid off. Shortly after narrowly escaping a knife-wielding assailant, Joe encounters Ruth, who assumes Joe saved him from an assassination attempt and therefore invites him and his father to join the momentous travels. The father capitalizes on the encounter by securing Ruth’s autograph on a bundle of baseballs, a personal milestone fulfilled, while Joe seizes the chance to be present at the game he hoped to witness. Amidst the excitement, the elder Stoshack spots Franklin D. Roosevelt, a presidential hopeful at the time who would be elected just a month later, and attempts to warn him about looming atrocities. Security, mistaking him for a potential assassin, detains him. Meanwhile, Joe watches the game and confirms Ruth’s famed signal, then rejoins his father. Although the signed baseballs are confiscated, the reunion with his son is the true reward for the elder Stoshack, who cherishes the rare moment they shared. Returning to the present, Joe delivers a Walk-Off homer in his own Little League game, echoing Ruth’s legendary shot.

While Stephanie searches for Kenny, a friend of his is fatally shot in the head, complicating the investigation. Lula—who previously appeared as a hooker in One for the Money—takes a job as a file clerk at Vinnie’s Bail Bonds, though she quickly decides that teaming with Stephanie is more compelling than filing papers. Stephanie then speaks with Spiro Stiva, the son of the local funeral home owner and Mancuso’s longtime friend from childhood. Stiva asks for Stephanie’s help locating twenty-four bargain-basement caskets that have vanished, along with assorted body parts. As events unfold, embalmed remains begin appearing in Stephanie’s apartment, accompanied by threatening notes. Simultaneously, several weapons disappear from a military site. In the end, Stephanie and Grandma Mazur find themselves trapped in the basement of Stiva’s Funeral Home and ignite a fire to escape. Their Jeep Wrangler—Sahara, stolen outside Eternal Slumber on Stark Street—likely winds up at a chop shop.

In a desolate, sunless future where perpetual cloud cover blocks the sky, Elsha is a teenage girl living among stark social division. Humanity has split into two strata: the Chosen and the Quelled, with Elsha belonging to the latter, condemned to lifelong subjugation as miners of the planet’s only warmth—firestones. The Firelord, revered as a formidable ruler of the Chosen, oversees this harsh order. When Elsha’s rebellious spirit leads her toward execution, a Chosen man named Amasai—Steward to the Firelord—intervenes, elevating her to the highest role open to a woman: Handmaiden to the Firelord. During her travels with the Firelord, Elsha encounters Teraj, who is later revealed to be the Firelord’s son, and she and Teraj begin a romance. From her unique position, Elsha challenges the prejudice and oppression facing her people, and after the Firelord’s sudden death, she ultimately inherits the leadership herself, steering the planet toward a better future. It is suggested that she marries Teraj. *Out of Print*

Barton Royal, a stout 40-something with a fixation on boys, resides in Los Angeles but often travels out of state to kidnap a suitable young male for a so-called fatherhood bond. In an Iowa mall, he fixes his sights on 12-year-old Billy Neary, shadows him home, abducts him late at night, and hauls Billy back to California, the boy strapped into the rear of a Aerostar minivan. The story intermittently reveals Barton's unhappy, abusive childhood at the hands of his father, and he recalls his own misdeeds toward other boys prior to Billy. During the escape attempts, Billy manages to make several phone calls, both during the journey and after arriving at Barton's residence. Barton vacillates between brutal violence and periods of self-deception. Inside Barton's lair, nicknamed the black room, Billy stumbles upon the skeletal remains of numerous other boys. Ultimately, Billy's father learns of his location and reaches the pursuing authorities before Barton can inflict further torture or murder.

Set in a 1968 New York that diverges from the Dryco series’ canon, Going, Going, Gone still resolves several recurring characters in its final chapters. Its central figure is Walter Bullitt, a self-centered expert on psychoactive substances who moonlights for multiple branches of the U.S. government’s intelligence apparatus. Although he appears white, Bullitt is actually of African descent in a world where nearly all full-blooded Black people perished in an engineered plague during the early twentieth century, and where Black music is banned. As the narrative unfolds, Walter experiences increasingly surreal phenomena—voices, apparitions from a parallel New York that begins to intrude upon his own reality. He is drawn into this alternate city, which has been flooded, shifted north, and now houses Black communities and a TV analogue missing from his universe. The story culminates with the two epistemic realms merging into a single New York, which critic Paul Dukes calls a morally superior place than either antecedent world could stand as.

Nell Cardross, the young, beautiful wife of the Earl of Cardross, serves as the central figure in April Lady. Although she hails from a respectable family that social circles welcome, her father and brother live beyond their means, and the clan’s finances are strained. The Earl, considerably older and seasoned by society, is wealthy and decidedly attractive, and he has his pick of the season’s debutantes. He falls for Nell instantly and, despite friends’ cautions about her family’s gambling tendencies, immediately asks for her hand. Nell’s mother, described as having “more hair than wit,” warns that Cardross desires an heir and wants to wed into a solid lineage. She advises Nell to become a compliant wife and not trouble her husband. Thus, Nell—who reciprocates his feelings from their first moment of meeting—keeps her distance as their marriage begins. Cardross, in turn, begins to doubt her appeal, and the couple remain at odds for months, a stalemate in which the dynamics are aided by Cardross’s half-sister and her fiancé Jeremy, Nell’s brother Dysart, and Cardross’s cousin Felix. Ultimately, the tension resolves in a favorable, happily-ever-after outcome.

Chester W. Chester IV inherits a run-down mansion and millions in back taxes. In order to pay the taxes, he initially decides to auction off the mansion and its contents, including a massive computer (the Generalized Nonlinear Extrapolator, or "Genie"). However, while examining the mansion and the computer with his friend Case Mulvihill, he finds the computer can solve complex problems involving historical fact and display realistic images of them. He hits on the idea of using its capabilities to create an elaborate hoax ... a fake time machine. Accordingly, he asks the computer to show him "real, three-D, big as life dinosaurs and plenty of em - and how about a four-wall presentation?" The computer asks if it should employ a method of doing so that "is a purely theoretical approach, which might prove simpler, if feasible, and would perhaps provide total verisimilitude..." Chester tells the computer to "go to it" and the computer does. However, the computer has managed to actually transport the two through time, and on their second trip back, before they realize that they actually do have a time machine, they make the mistake of leaving their arrival area, and become trapped in the past. Even when they manage to return to the present, their actions in the past have altered it completely, but they are able to use the computer to (perhaps, more or less) restore everything to the way it was.

This 32-page book begins with a two-page introduction. According to the adventure background provided, the plot involves a fortress that became buried in the earth ages ago, and became known as the Sunless Citadel. In the citadel's core grows the terrible Gulthias Tree, shepherded by the twisted druid, Belak the Outcast. The Tree spawns magical life giving (and life stealing) fruit, as well as evil creatures known as twig blights. The adventure starts with player characters hearing rumors about the citadel while staying in the nearby small town of Oakhurst. The majority of the adventure then focuses on the characters exploring the citadel and encountering the malign creatures that have taken up residence within, such as kobolds and goblins. The characters eventually come upon the Twilight Grove and its blighted foliage, where they find the Gulthias Tree and encounter the druid Belak. He explains that the tree grew from a yet-green wooden stake that had been used to kill a vampire on that very spot, and the tree accepts humanoids bound to its bole as "supplicants", making the victims completely subservient to its will. A three-page appendix at the back of the book features statistics for all of the creatures encountered in the adventure, as well as three new magic items and the twig blights.

Two converging narratives thread through the tale of Francis Petrel, a man newly released from an asylum who wrestles with his inner demons while recalling a murder that occurred within those walls. Half of the story unfolds as a memory resurfacing—Petrel in his asylum confines, memories gradually reassembling into clarity. The other half follows him after discharge, driven to write a book recounting the surrounding events of the killing. Lacking paper, he inscribes his account directly on the wall, facing constant, tedious interruptions that hinder progress. In tandem, he abandons his medication, and the mounting strain of finishing the manuscript collides with his battle against madness. Plans for a film adaptation exist, with production slated to begin roughly from November 26, 2007, to about January 20, 2008, at Fairfield State Hospital in Newtown, Connecticut. However, shooting has stalled due to the lead actor Jonathan Rhys Meyers’s personal issues, as reported by the Newtown Bee. An interesting note from the text’s descriptions suggests that the central hospital, Western State Hospital, closely resembles Northampton State Hospital, which operated in Northampton, Massachusetts, from 1856 to 1996.

Griffin Moss is an artist living in London who makes postcards for a living. He is unhappy and lonely, though he is unaware of these feelings. His life is changed forever when he receives a cryptic postcard from Sabine Strohem, a woman he has never met. Like Griffin, she is an artist (she illustrates postage stamps) and comes from a fictional group of small islands in the South Pacific known as the Sicmon Islands (Arbah, Katie, Katin, Ta Fin, Quepol and Typ). The two begin to correspond regularly. Griffin comes to realize that he is in love with Sabine, who reciprocates his feelings, and that they are soulmates. However, his growing uncertainty as to Sabine's true nature and the changes her presence in his life has brought to him develops into fear and he ends up rejecting her offer for him to come see her in person. He comes to the conclusion that Sabine is a figment of his imagination, created from his own loneliness. It appears to be true until another postcard arrives from Sabine with an ominous promise that if he will not come to her, she will go to him.

Igraine lives in an old castle with her family, magicians who possess powerful books of magic. Her older brother Albert is following in the family line, but Igraine plans to be a knight one day, even though she feels there is not much adventure to be had at home these days. Her ancestors, though, had warded off many attempts to steal the books of magic. On her 12th birthday, Igraine's parents give her a magical suit of armor, but in the process, they are turned into pigs by mistake. Matters get worse when the next-door Baroness's castle is taken over by Osmond the Greedy, who wants to take the magical books so he can overthrow the king. Igraine and her brother must find a way to defend the castle from Osmond's siege while keeping their parents' condition secret and searching for the missing ingredient for their restoration to human form. Albert handles the castle's magical defenses while Igraine leaves to find the missing ingredient. She finds the ingredient and some assistance, in the form of the Sorrowful Knight of the Mount of Tears, who not only agrees to help her return home but also begins teaching her about the rules of chivalry, and eventually helps Igraine and her family end the siege.

A young Conan Finds himself drawn into schemes aimed at dethroning the ruler of Khauran. After rescuing Lady Khashtris from an assault by thieves from Shadizar and a cadre of treacherous accomplices, Conan agrees to serve as her bodyguard in exchange for freedom from the mirror that has trapped his soul since his encounter with Hissar Zul. The plan hinges on a release by someone of noble birth, and Khashtris convinces him that Queen Ialamis—the sister she longs to appeal to—will grant his liberation. Unbeknownst to Conan, Khashtris, and the Queen, the Queen’s latest lover, Sergianus, is in fact Sabaninus, the aged Duke of Korveka. Korveka governs a Kothian province seeking to annex Khauran, and his true identity is masked by a disguise. The disguise falls away when the Queen shatters the mirror that contains Conan’s soul; as his spirit re-enters his body, Conan recognizes the Duke’s true nature. Together with Lady Khashtris and her steadfast bodyguard Shubal, Conan sets out to expose the Duke and safeguard Khauran. It is also noted that Ialamis is the mother of Salome and Taramis, figures who appear prominently in Howard’s Conan story, “A Witch Shall Be Born.”

A scientific expedition from Earth reaches the Crab Nebula only to collide with another spaceship pursuing the same objective: an alien vessel that bears humanoid traits, differing in some details (notably that it communicates by microwaves instead of sound). Yet the two crews reveal many commonalities, including a shared sense of humor, and soon establish a working means of dialogue. Despite their rapport, both sides fear the other could be sent home with knowledge that might enable its destruction. Months slip by with a stalemate persisting between the ships. In a breakthrough, a junior human scientist proposes a risky plan: exchange the vessels and, crucially, erase all records of each crew’s homeworld so that neither side can identify or pursue the other. Thus the proposal would let both groups return home without annihilating one another. This story, First Contact, was selected in 1970 by the Science Fiction Writers of America as one of the finest pre-Nebula Award short stories, leading to its inclusion in The Science Fiction Hall of Fame Volume One, 1929-1964.

A psychiatric patient has lost his way and arrives at the country of Kappa. He is treated as a special guest and talks with Kappas of many occupations. Geeru, a radical capitalist, states that the unemployed labourers of Kappas are killed and their flesh is provided for food. The patient is astonished but Geeru argues that because the Japanese women in the poorest class are obliged to survive by prostitution, the patient's opposition is sentimental. Kappa's national characteristics are materialism and nihilistic realism. The babies of Kappa control their destiny. While in the womb, the fetus can refuse life as a Kappa, and be aborted. The Maggu, the sceptical philosopher Kappa committed suicide and appears as a ghost through the person of Tokku, a poet. Maggu is concerned about his fame after his death, although he admires the writers and philosophers who has died by suicide such as Heinrich von Kleist and Otto Weininger. At last the patient is due to return to the real human world, but muses that Kappa was clean and superior to human society and becomes a misanthrope.

Oliver Russell, a man with a desire for power, is fated to rise to the highest office, that of President of the United States. Leslie Stewart, his betrayed fiancée, is a woman dedicated to the single purpose of bringing Oliver Russell to ruin. After amassing her own media empire and marshaling all her forces against him, she stands poised to destroy Russell on the eve of his most dazzling triumph. Thinking only of preventing Oliver from winning the Presidency for a second term, little does she know that she is about to fall into her own trap. When Oliver returns from Paris married to Jan, Leslie vows to avenge him. However she keeps her thoughts concealed. This makes Todd Davis, Jan's father, introduce her to one of his friends, who owns a newspaper. A brief introduction followed by marriage sees Leslie manage her husband's empire. With his falling health and subsequent death, Leslie becomes the sole owner of his properties. In spite of all the other businesses, Leslie takes an immense liking for the media empire, with which she intends to destroy Oliver. During this part, Dana Evans, who stars in Sheldon's other novel "Sky is Falling," appears as an inquisitive reporter who adopts a boy from war torn Sarajevo. In the meantime, Oliver becomes the president, but during his first term there occur a series of deaths, all due to toxicity of Liquid Ecstasy, a dangerous aphrodisiac that Leslie connects to him. When she is convinced it is Oliver who is behind these murders, she goes on to publish the news of his arrest before it is confirmed. Dana Evans then unmasks the real culprit, while the president reveals a shocking secret. The book ends with the proposal of a peace pact, brokered by President Russell, among the Arab nations, while Leslie is left wondering if she has gone a bit too far.

In 1998, Travis Boyette abducted, raped, and buried Nikki Yarber, a teenage high school student from Slone, Texas, in a shallow grave near Joplin, Missouri—about six hours away. He calmly watches as Donté Drumm, a Black high school football player with no connection to the crime, is arrested, tried, and convicted. Despite his innocence, Drumm receives a death sentence and remains on death row for nine years at the time of the events described. While Drumm endures imprisonment, attorney Robbie Flak fights to overturn his conviction and a backlash among Black Americans erupts, sparking a tense law-and-order climate. Meanwhile, Boyette has fled to Kansas, where he has lived since then, and his health has been failing due to a brain tumor that has worsened over nine years. As Drumm’s scheduled execution nears in 2007, Boyette, reflecting on his ruined life, resolves to do the right thing: he confesses. A priest, Reverend Keith Schroeder, accompanies him back to Slone to reveal the truth. Even after Boyette’s public confession, the state proceeds with Drumm’s execution by lethal injection. Only then does Boyette disclose Nikki’s burial site, and DNA testing later confirms marks of rape and assault on her remains.

The Discworld part of the book begins when a new experimental power source for the Unseen University is commissioned in the university's squash court. The new "reactor" is capable of splitting the thaum (the basic particle of magic), in homage to the Chicago Pile-1 nuclear reactor, which was housed in a rackets court at the University of Chicago. However, the wizards' new reactor produces vastly more magical energy than planned and threatens to explode, destroying the University, the Discworld, and the entire universe. The university's thinking engine, Hex, decides to divert all the magic into creating a space containing nothing — no matter, no energy, no reality, and, importantly, no magic. The Dean sticks his fingers in the space and "twiddles" them, inadvertently creating the universe. The wizards soon discover that they can move things around in the universe, using Hex. They call it the Roundworld (the Earth), because in it, matter seems to accrete into balls in space (instead of discs on the backs of turtles). They decide to appoint Rincewind, whom they dragged out of bed in the early hours of the morning, the Egregious Professor of Cruel and Unusual Geography, and send him down (against his will) to investigate this strange world. The wizards create a series of balls of matter in space, and give one of them a Moon (accidentally). This stabilizes the ball enough that, over a score of millennia (the wizards can skip over vast periods of Roundworld time, allowing them to view the history of the universe in less than a month), blobs of life emerge, ready to begin evolving into more complex forms. The book also features a fictional crab civilization and the dinosaurs (both of which are wiped out by comets/asteroids colliding with the earth), before jumping ahead to when an advanced civilization (presumably humans) has evacuated the earth due to an impending natural disaster.

Set during the reign of King Charles II, the narrative follows Quaker leader Rowland Ellis and his journey from Wales to founding a Welsh settlement in Pennsylvania after religious persecution drove him abroad. A sequel, Y Rhandir Mwyn (The Gentle Region), continues the tale. Ellis becomes a Quaker under a neighbor’s influence, though his wife remains outside the faith. After her death, he weds a sympathetic cousin. A servant he has dismissed betrays him to the authorities, claiming to have seen a hidden chamber in Ellis’s house filled with Catholic worship objects. Yet the title The Secret Room signals more than this alleged secret: it also points to the private chamber within the heart where the inner light resides. Ellis and his fellow Quakers are jailed and illegally sentenced to death, but the king personally intervenes to secure their release. Despite this reprieve, they opt to leave Wales and seek a livelihood in America. cy:Y Stafell Ddirgel

The tale unfolds as Ender earns the role of Dragon Army’s commander at Battle School, an academy aimed at molding young pupils into military leaders for an upcoming interstellar conflict against an unnamed foe. In Battle Room, where gravity is null, cohorts of students engage in simulated warfare, organized into squads called “toons.” Ender’s exceptional leadership quickly makes Dragon Army dominant, despite teachers continually stacking obstacles in their path. After achieving nineteen straight victories, Ender learns his unit will be disbanded; his toons will rise as commanders in their own right, and he himself will be sent to Command School for further training. There he encounters Mazer Rackham, a seasoned veteran who introduces him to a space-battle simulator. With time, many of his former toon leaders rejoin him as his subordinates. As they grow accustomed to the simulator, they participate in a sequence of battles that Mazer characterizes as mock confrontations against a computer-ruled adversary. Ender’s squad repeatedly triumphs, ultimately destroying a planet that the hostile fleet appears to shield. When the ordeal ends, the exhausted Ender is told by Mazer that the battles were not simulations at all: the commands issued by the children were being transmitted to a real fleet, and Ender has just annihilated the enemy’s home world, thereby ending the war.

Thirty-five-year-old Michiel (Michael) Steyn returns to the family farm in South Africa for his mother’s funeral, marking his first trip back in fifteen years since he fled in 1987 to escape a scandal tied to his service as a naval officer. Of mixed Afrikaans and English heritage, Steyn has become a United States citizen and now shares a life with his partner, Kamil Cassis, who is of Palestinian and Jewish heritage, on the edge of San Francisco’s Castro district. The novel centers on South African themes—racism, guilt, accountability, and the fragility of forgiveness—while its finale pushes readers toward an international lens, notably through foreshadowing US foreign and domestic policy in the George W. Bush era. Kings of the Water also recalls an older incarnation of a marginal figure from Embrace and nods to the extended fishing sequence in The Smell of Apples, thereby inviting readers to interpret all three works in a connected dialogue.

Eleven-year-old Josie travels to upstate New York to live with her great-aunt after her mother abandons her father for no clear reason. There, she encounters Jared, her 25-year-old cousin who is training to become a minister. Josie’s stay proves to be deeply distressing: she endures physical and psychological abuse from both her mother and great-aunt, and she faces relentless bullying at school. Rejected by her mother, she yearns for affection and turns toward Jared for solace. But his intentions are cruel in disguise; he feigns care to manipulate her into self-harm, into drinking her own blood, and into viewing explicit material, subjecting her to his verbal torment. Soon his sexual abuse begins, which Josie mistakes for genuine love even as she recognizes the wrongdoing. Her realization grows about her mother’s incapacity for love, traced to her mother’s enduring lack of admiration for Josie’s father and other men. After an extended stay, Josie’s mental state deteriorates, likely due to her illicit relationship with Jared. In a pivotal moment by a creek, the two initiate sexual activity; Jared then cuts his chest with a stone, Josie licks the bleeding wound, and he dies from blood loss. This constitutes the novella’s climax. Ultimately, Josie escapes the mansion, breaking free from Jared’s imprisonment.

In Remix Lawrence Lessig, a Harvard law professor and a respected voice in what he deems the "copyright wars", describes the disjuncture between the availability and relative simplicity of remix technologies and copyright law. Lessig insists that copyright law as it stands now is antiquated for digital media since every "time you use a creative work in a digital context, the technology is making a copy" (98). Thus, amateur use and appropriation of digital technology is under unprecedented control that previously extended only to professional use. Lessig insists that knowledge and manipulation of multi-media technologies is the current generation's form of "literacy"- what reading and writing was to the previous. It is the vernacular of today. The children growing up in a world where these technologies permeate their daily life are unable to comprehend why "remixing" is illegal. Lessig insists that amateur appropriation in the digital age cannot be stopped but only 'criminalized'. Thus most corrosive outcome of this tension is that generations of children are growing up doing what they know is "illegal" and that notion has societal implications that extend far beyond copyright wars. The book is now available as a free download under one of the Creative Commons' licenses.

An Open Swimmer unfolds in three parts as a coming‑of‑age tale centered on Jerra Nilsam, a late‑teenager. Much of the narrative follows a camping excursion he takes with his childhood friend Sean. During that trip, the pair encounter an old man who lives in a shack by the beach near their campground. As events unfold, it becomes clear that this man previously killed his wife in a similar shack on a neighboring shore by setting the place ablaze with her inside. The novel is threaded with numerous subplots—delivered in brief, spontaneous paragraphs and dialogue among unnamed figures that presumably include Jerra. After returning home and drifting apart from Sean, Jerra goes back to the campsite alone. While he sleeps in his van, a violent storm rages, toppled a large tree onto the Kombi, and the storm subsides with Jerra waking up in the old man’s hut, having been rescued by the same man. In the closing moment, Jerra reappears at his Kombi, opens the fuel tank, and casts a lit match inside before fleeing.

A group of migrant laborers from three continents flees their English strawberry fields to traverse England in pursuit of diverse dreams of a better future. The narrative follows workers from Eastern Europe, China, Malaysia, and Africa who have gathered in Kent to harvest berries bound for supermarkets, eventually living in two small caravans—one for men and one for women. Each is seeking a better life, and, in their own ways, seeking love as well, having arrived in England—some legally, some illegally—to pursue those aims. Their overseer is Farmer Leapish, a ruddy-faced man who treats everyone equally except Yola, a Polish woman who leads the crew and indulges him with flirtations in exchange for a bit of extra on the side. Their arrangement remains discreet, and the atmosphere in this tranquil vale seems harmonious until a fateful evening when Leapish’s wife stumbles upon him with Yola and, in retaliation, rams him with her red sports car. After the police are summoned, the migrant workers (along with a dog named Dog) hurry into one of the trailer homes and abandon their idyllic refuge, embarking on a wide-ranging journey across England.

The year is 1934, and Nick, stuck writing scripts for a film company without notable success, receives an invitation from his colleague Chips Lovell to attend a party hosted by Lady Molly Jeavons. There, he learns that Widmerpool is set to wed Mildred Haycock, a woman who is twice widowed and regarded by some as notorious—or even a bit mad, in Nick’s view. The luncheon with Widmerpool and the ambush of questions from Widmerpool’s future in‑laws quickly become a recurring motif for Nick throughout the novel. At the same gathering, the familiar Alfred Tolland makes another appearance. A chance encounter with Quiggin at a cinema showing Man of Aran leads to an unexpected and enigmatic invitation to spend a weekend out in the country. It turns out Quiggin and Mona Templer are staying in a cottage lent by Erridge, Lord Warminster and the eccentric head of the Tolland clan. While there, the group visits Thrubworth Park, the Tolland ancestral home, for a modest but eventful dinner. As the meal nears its end, two Tolland sisters, Susan and Isobel, arrive. Later, Nick crosses paths with Lady Molly’s husband, Ted Jeavons, in a Soho pub, and the pair head to Umfraville’s nightclub, where they encounter Widmerpool—whose jaundice has flared up again—along with Mrs. Haycock and Templer. In the autumn of 1934, Jenkins becomes engaged to Isobel. Erridge, intent on personally observing conditions, travels to China amid Japanese military offensives, while Mona accompanies him, leaving Quiggin behind. Widmerpool’s engagement to Mildred Haycock ends in a ridiculous—and, for most men, crushing—disappointment, yet Widmerpool remains unfazed. Adapted, in part, from material published by the Anthony Powell Society with their consent.”

In Oppenheimer’s account, the origin of modern humans traces to Africa, where both the emergence of Homo sapiens and the onset of modern behavior occurred before any Out of Africa displacement. He argues there was a single migratory event out of Africa that seeded populations across the globe. From the Horn of Africa, anatomically modern humans are said to have crossed the Red Sea and then advanced along the southern coastal corridor in Asia. Consequently, he disputes the alternative hypothesis proposed by Lahr and Foley (1994) of a separate northern out-of-Africa route through the Nile and into the Levant. The text also supports the idea that modern humans inhabited South Asia during the time of the Toba catastrophe. To describe genetic lineages, Oppenheimer employs well-known biblical names for the most recent common ancestors inferred from mitochondrial DNA and the Y chromosome, while other paternal lines are labeled Cain, Abel, and Seth. Mitochondrial haplogroups are frequently named with female identifiers drawn from regions where those groups are common—for instance, haplogroup M is called Manju because it is prevalent in India, and haplogroup N is called Nasreen as it predominates in Arabia.

Set in a vaguely futuristic society dominated by The Game—a brutal fusion of rock music and violence performed by the Markers under The Keepers’ control—the play follows Hoss as he battles to be the top Marker. Facing rival Gypsies who flout official rules, he begins to doubt himself. In Act I, his eagerness to go out clashes with Star-Man’s astrology-based cautions. News arrives that Mojo Root Force threatens his Las Vegas turf in a questionable maneuver, and when a Gypsy from Vegas is en route to attack, Hoss reaches out to old ally Little Willard for help. Discovering that Willard has committed suicide from the pressure of his status compounds Hoss’s insecurities and his sense that the old order is ending. He tries to shore up his courage by challenging the Gypsy to a shiv duel, which marks a shift in tone. Act II opens with the duel’s format altered to a verbal contest supervised by a referee. Hoss and Crow engage in psychological games, with Crow mimicking Hoss’s gait and mannerisms while Hoss taunts him with the voice of a seasoned Western gunslinger. A later turn, in which Hoss adopts the persona of a Delta bluesman, seems to give him an edge, yet Crow exposes a persistent fear that he might shatter. After the referee is killed, a desperate Hoss pleads with Crow to teach him the new technique. In the end, he chooses to perform one final act of authenticity by taking his own life, a moment Crow approves. The curtain falls with Crow occupying Hoss’s throne as Becky swiftly shifts her allegiance.

Miranda is sixteen and concerned with being sensible, while Cassandra, nine years and eleven months, likes and believes in magical things. Miranda is outnumbered in this family, because Professor Aisling lectures on mythology and legends at his university, and believes in mysterious and magical things too. But some of the members of the university think that it is nonsense to teach about myths and legends, because magical and mysterious things cannot be dissected, weighed and measured. One member in particular, Mr. Bilgewallow, takes delight in tormenting Professor Aisling, who wishes, and dreams, of a ship that would take him to the worlds where he might find the creatures of legend. One evening, his wish comes true. As he and his daughters walk along the river, they come across a curious little ship, with a crew of dwarfs and gremlins. One of the dwarfs introduces himself as Malachi, Captain of H.M.S. Basset. He says that it is Professor Aisling's ship, conjured from his wishes and ready to sail on the "tides of inspiration." Aisling is astonished and delighted, and he and Cassandra waste no time in going aboard. Miranda needs a bit more coaxing. The Aislings set sail on a magical voyage where they meet a number of creatures from mythology that join them on board the ship. Included among these are the Harpies, who take over the galley, the Manticore, the Sphinx, the Minotaur and a dryad, complete with tree. Disaster strikes when Aisling becomes distracted by the potential of bringing back measurable proof for Bilgewallow and his ilk. He also insists on bringing the lovely but deadly Medusa on board, with predictable results for one of the crew. But through the help of his daughters and Medusa, he recovers his belief and his balance, as all of them must unite against the evil trolls who pursue him.

_ The book concerns an elephant named Horton, who is convinced by Mayzie (a lazy, irresponsible bird) to sit on her egg while she takes a short "break", which in actuality ends up being Mayzie's permanent relocation to Palm Beach. Naturally, the absurd sight of an elephant sitting atop a tree makes quite a scene – Horton is exposed to the elements, laughed at by his jungle friends, captured by hunters, forced to endure a terrible sea voyage, and finally placed in a traveling circus. However, despite his hardships and Mayzie's clear intent not to return, Horton refuses to leave the nest through all of these, because he insists on keeping his word ("I meant what I said and I said what I meant, And an elephant's faithful, one hundred per cent!") The traveling circus ends up visiting near Mayzie's new Palm Beach residence; she returns to the circus once the egg is due to hatch, and demands its return without offering any reward for Horton. However, when the egg hatches, the creature that emerges is an "elephant-bird" cross between Horton and Mayzie, and Horton and the baby are returned happily to the jungle, rewarding Horton for his persistence, while Mayzie is punished for her laziness by ending up with nothing.

Lieutenant Bret Taylor married his wife after knowing her only over a single overnight drinking binge while on shore leave during the war. His ship is bombed out of the water and he returns home to find his wife freshly murdered in the home he bought but had never seen. The shock of the two events sends him into a mental lapse, and he's in an asylum. The woman who loves him, a successful screenwriter, calls in a specialist who jogs his memory—and his sense of duty. Taylor hits the streets of Los Angeles, digging through his wife's lies and lovers in an attempt to avenge her murder. The book is a psychological thriller, with the main action being the unraveling of the story within Taylor's mind. The reader is denied information that other major characters obviously have throughout the whole novel, and is meanwhile treated to long passages of theories from the main character. The limited number of characters keeps the possible solutions to a minimum and the book is perhaps more straightforward than what makes a good mystery. Alfred A. Knopf, Jr., who functioned as an editing publisher, asked for revisions in what he considered a slow-paced novel. Macdonald cut '10,000 good words' and concentrated the action into four days. The 1985 movie Deadly Companion (or Double Negative) was based on this novel.

Bernard, a former Catholic priest now living secularly, escorts his reluctant father, Jack, to Hawaii at the urging of his dying aunt Ursula. Shortly after they arrive, a car strikes Jack, sending him to the hospital. While he tends to Jack at the hospital and then balances time at Ursula’s nursing home, Bernard gradually uncovers the family’s hidden past. Ursula, long cast as the selfish outcast, reveals that she was sexually abused by her eldest brother Sean, a figure the family idolized for his wartime heroism. The revelation explains how the trauma wrecked Ursula’s marriage and life, and she urges Jack to offer forgiveness—aware that he knew about the abuse but remained silent. Amid these revelations, Bernard begins a cautious romance with Yolande Miller, the woman who drove the car that struck his father. His own sexual awakening unfolds in tandem with Ursula’s battle with illness. The storytelling shifts among multiple formats: third-person narration, Bernard’s diary, a lengthy letter Bernard writes to Yolande, and a collection of postcards and notes sent from Hawaii by characters they encounter on the plane journey from England. The narrative closes with a final letter from Yolande to Bernard.

Set aboard the Sky pirate vessel The Galerider, the tale follows Wind Jackal as he seeks vengeance against his former quartermaster, Turbot Smeal, whom he blames for burning Western Quays in Undertown and for devastating much of Wind Jackal’s family. Simultaneously, Undertown’s Leagues prepare to wage war on the sky pirates. Along the voyage, The Galerider’s crew confront a series of perilous traps as Wind Jackal presses on with his search for Smeal. Though the crew is initially perplexed, the truth gradually unfolds: the man posing as Turbot Smeal is a counterfeit, driven by envy and far more dangerous. By the end, only Wind Jackal, Quint, Tem Barkwater, and Spillins the Oakelf remain from the original squad. They stumble upon a wrecked skyship where a skullpelt-masked stranger claims to be Turbot Smeal. A duel ensues between Wind Jackal and the impostor, resulting in Wind Jackal’s death. The mystery is clarified when the masked man is revealed to be Thaw Daggerslash, one of the crew members. The narrative culminates with a dramatic skyborne confrontation between the Leagues of Undertown and the Sky Pirates, culminating in the Leagues’ launch of the Bringer of Doom during the climactic sequence. The ultimate truth of the story is disclosed at the end. All told, the tale centers on betrayal, warfare among aerial factions, and a final, spectacular clash in the heavens.

Suicide Circle: The Complete Edition tells in four different chapters the story behind a fictional mass suicide that takes place on the Shinjuku Station in 2002, on which 54 high school girls throw themselves in front of a train. This event unleashes in Japan—and soon after, in the world—a chain of suicides that seems endless. Police officers try to stop it and understand why this is happening, and after several events they find a connection between the suicides and a website that belongs to a mysterious organization called Family Circle. Through this website, Family Circle enrolls young people and incite them to run away from home to serve the Circle "family rentals", a service that the organization provides to families who lost relatives to suicide. Parallel to this, alongside the police's quest, the book also follows the story of one of Family Circle's new members that witnessed the mass suicide, Noriko Shimabara, and how her own family slowly falls apart to the suicide wave, while her father tries to "rescue" her from the Circle. In the end, all the pieces come together as the true meaning behind the website is revealed.

On Christmas Eve, Ricky Bianca confronts the haunting question of why his father chose to end his life. At the time, his father was opposing mob influence over the funeral trade, a conflict that ran deep. A man loyal to the Mafia arrived with a letter on the sacred night, and after reading it, Ricky’s father shot himself in the head. The document disappeared, and only the Crime Family’s capo di tutti capi, Salvatore Biganti, knows its contents. When the blast rang out, Ricky hurried to help, finding his father collapsed and bleeding from a fatal wound near the temple. He knelt amid the crimson slick, trying in vain to staunch the bleeding as he cradled his father’s head. The aftermath left Ricky with no memory of the moment, yet plagued by violent, surreal nightmares. His mother soon died in an upstate sanitarium, overcome by severe depressive catatonia. His aunt in Connecticut raised him, and after two decades he returns to New York to work as a Funeral Director, drawn back into the very world that guards its secrets. A college psychology professor, a friend, urges him to uncover the truths his mind desperately seeks before the hallucinatory torment consumes him. Darkness closes in as the industry’s web of deceit, greed, and malevolence ensnares him, stripping away his innocence. He becomes entangled in a perilous lattice of organized crime, secret cults, and unspeakable horrors. In the end, what is known proves more terrifying than what remains hidden, driving him into a personal hell of fiendish nightmares and monstrous visions.

Trelawny of the 'Wells tells the story of Rose Trelawny, a popular star of melodrama plays at the Barridge Wells Theatre (a thinly disguised Sadler's Wells Theatre). Rose gives up the stage when she decides to marry her sweetheart, Arthur Gower, in order to please his conservative family. She finds life with Arthur's grandfather and great-aunt, Sir William and Lady Tralfagar, unbearably dull and they detest her loud and unrestrained personality. Rose runs back to the theatre, abandoning Arthur. But her experience of the 'real world' has killed her talent for melodrama, and she cannot recapture the liveliness that had made her a star. Meanwhile, Arthur has secretly run away to become an actor at the Bristol Old Vic. The problem is solved when Rose encounters Sir William again, and she reawakens his memory of admiring the great actor Edmund Kean as a young man. Sir William offers to help Rose's friend Tom Wrench, an aspiring playwright who dreams of staging plays in a more realist style than the melodramas that dominate the stage. Tom stages the play with Rose as the star, and her newfound seriousness fits his style perfectly. Tom secretly arranges for Arthur to play the leading male role, and the lovers are reunited on stage.

The work unfolds in three major segments—preceded by a short prologue and bookended by interludes and an epilogue—each centering on the silver tiassa statue and the figure of Khaavren from House Tiassa, yet each one narrates a different tale. The opening portion, titled Tag, recounts events from Vlad Taltos’s early career as a prominent Jhereg, told in his characteristic first-person voice. In this part, Vlad is approached by the Viscount of Adrilhanka, a rogue highwayman, who seeks Vlad’s help to foil a plot by the Empire to recover pilfered funds. Jumping to a later moment in the chronology, the second section, Whitecrest, follows several characters after Vlad has fallen out with the Jhereg: most prominently, the Countess of Whitecrest—Khaavren’s wife and the Viscount’s mother—and Vlad’s former wife, Cawti. Here, news of an impending Jenoine invasion surfaces, though the threat might be a feint designed to lure Vlad into the open. The final segment, Special Tasks, represents the most recent timeline and adopts the voice of Paarfi, the fictional author shaping the Khaavren Romances. Its focus is largely on Khaavren as he investigates an attempt on Vlad’s life.

The tales of Fafhrd and the Gray Mouser center on two charming yet thieving rogues as they wander the fantasy realm of Nehwon. In Swords Against Death, their adventures begin with shedding Lankhmar’s dust in the wake of their first loves’ deaths, only to discover that choosing not to return cannot truly be a solution ("The Circle Curse"). What follows is a loose sequence of exploits from their travels: a treasure-seeking expedition inside a dwelling protected by uncanny defenses ("The Jewels in the Forest"), another confrontation with the Thieves’ Guild blamed for the deaths of their beloveds ("Thieves’ House"), a spellbound voyage to a distant realm ("The Bleak Shore"), an encounter with a lone, beast-haunted wanderer ("The Howling Tower"), a perilous sojourn to a Nehwonan Atlantis-like site ("The Sunken Land"), a clash with a murderous priesthood ("The Seven Black Priests"), a magical plague menacing Lankhmar ("Claws from the Night"), and at last a farewell to their lost loves in the Shadowland ("The Price of Pain-Ease"). The collection closes with an investigation of a mysterious shop that defies ordinary expectations, titled Bazaar of the Bizarre.

Toward the close of World War I, in 1918, the tale centers on Paul Peachy, a timid Milwaukee railway worker who moonlights as an amateur actor. After realizing his wife no longer loves him, he signs up as a private in the U.S. Army and sails to the French front. In the brutal melee of war he finds brief comfort in companionship, yet soon falls into German hands in No Man’s Land. His only hope of surviving hinges on impersonating a renowned enemy spy, a skill within his reach as a native speaker of German. Assuming the persona of the sophisticated operative Harry Stroller, Peachy earns the top brass’s admiration and enters a luxury world he had never imagined. The role also uncovers latent courage and resourcefulness, pushing him toward bolder ruses as his German hosts grow increasingly mistrustful. Amid this web of illusion, Peachy encounters Annie, a striking French courtesan who seems to see through his elaborate disguise. The narrative builds to an ending filled with twists and deft plotting.

During World War II, at a secret Nazi submarine base, containers crafted entirely from looted wartime gold were hidden away. The treasure was not the solid-gold chests, but the cargo they carried - an artifact so lethal that whoever possessed "Pandora's Boxes" held the power to unleash hell upon earth.... In the unforgiving wastes of Greenland, geologist Philip Mercer uncovers a long - abandoned U.S. Army base buried under the ice - and a long-dead body still hot with radiation. Before Mercer and his colleague, the seductive Dr. Anika Klein, can investigate further, a flash fire engulfs the base, and they are ordered to evacuate. But their plane is forced to land when a bomb is discovered on board, and they must seek shelter from the murderous weather in a hidden ice cavern. That's where they learn the startling truth. A powerful German corporation has launched an operation to destroy evidence of its Nazi past. But one of the corporate mercenaries knows what's inside the Pandora boxes, and he plans to hold the entire world hostage - unless Mercer can find a way to stop him....

Heartless blends steampunk aesthetics with urban fantasy, set in an alternate Victorian England where vampires and werewolves are embraced by society, often among the upper class. The narrative follows Alexia Tarabotti, known as the Lady Maccon, a soulless woman whose lack of a supernatural pulse renders her immune to the powers of beings of that world. In interviews, the author indicated that while Changeless and Blameless—the second and third books in the series—are tightly connected, Heartless stands more on its own, recalling the self-contained feel of Soulless, the series’ inaugural entry. The book was published in 2011 by Orbit Books, with the USA paperback released on June 28, 2011 (ISBN 0-316-12719-1) and the UK paperback following on July 7, 2011 (ISBN 0-356-50009-8). On September 22, 2010, the author announced the manuscript was 99% complete, with a final draft due to the publisher by November 1, 2010. Orbit Books unveiled the cover on February 1, 2011, and issued a revised version in late March 2011. As with the series’ first three novels, Lauren Panepinto designed the cover, featuring model Donna Ricci; Ricci’s original photographs for the cover were shot by Pixie Vision Productions. Although the author’s website lists translations into German, Italian, Spanish, and other languages as forthcoming, no publication dates have yet been announced for Heartless’ non-English editions.

Kwang Meng, an 18-year-old recent secondary-school graduate, frames the narrative as a young working adult navigating a dull clerical job. His life runs parallel to the divergent paths chosen by two old school friends: Hock Lai, who pursues a white-collar climb up the corporate ladder, and Portia (Nadarajah), who plans to study in the United Kingdom. A romance with a local bar girl named Lucy at Paradise Bar blossoms for a time, but their different social worlds compel Lucy to end things. In an effort to help, Hock Lai tries to arrange a match between Kwang Meng and one of his female acquaintances, Anne. Meanwhile, the neighborhood pair Boon Teik and Mei-I, both teachers, become part of Kwang Meng’s circle, and he envisions them as an ideal couple. Hock Lai marries Cecilia, the daughter of one of Singapore’s wealthy tycoons. Throughout the story, Kwang Meng remains largely passive, preferring to observe his surroundings and seek solace in sea swimming, smoking, and drinking. The novel closes with a personal upheaval as his father suffers a stroke, forcing the son to shoulder the family’s burdens moving forward.

Jean-Jacques Pauvert published Story of O in French, a narrative centered on female submission. It follows a Parisian fashion photographer known as O, who endures bondage, blindfolds, chains, whipping, branding, piercings, and wearing a mask, while being conditioned to remain constantly available for oral, vaginal, and anal sex. Throughout the ordeal, O’s prior permission is obtained for every act, and requests for consent are continually sought. The tale opens as her lover René takes her to the Roissy château, where she is trained to serve the men of an elite circle. After this initial phase, René entrusts O to Sir Stephen as a demonstration of their bond and his generosity, hoping she will learn to serve someone she does not love and who does not love her. During the training, O falls for Sir Stephen and comes to believe he loves her in return. While her superficial friend and former lover Jacqueline recoils from O’s chains and scars, O herself embraces pride in her role as a willing slave. In summer, Sir Stephen relocates O to Samois, a secluded mansion long used for women’s advanced training and body modification related to submission. There, she consents to branding and a labia piercing, receiving rings bearing Sir Stephen’s initials and insignia. The story culminates with O, naked save for an owl-like mask, appearing before a large audience that regards her solely as an object.

Set roughly four to five years after the events of Hip Hop High School, Homeboyz follows 17-year-old Dixon Theodore Anderson, known as Teddy. A bright, dual-tuned youth—both a hacker and a bodybuilder—he faces his neighborhood’s gang-ruled chaos, a reality that claims his sister Tina in crossfire. In the wake of her death, Teddy seeks vengeance, but his efforts falter and land him behind bars. He spends time in a California juvenile facility as his case moves through the courts, being treated as a gang figure during confinement. Released eventually, he enters house arrest and enters a probation program that redesigns his days. Five of those days each week are devoted to mentoring Micah, a younger boy he is supposed to guide. The tutoring proves tough because Micah longs for a gang life too, yet the relationship gradually teaches Teddy about love and the possibility of change in others. The narrative also recounts Teddy’s confrontation with Tina’s killer: not a member of his own 0-1-0 faction, but from a rival gang. After a fierce struggle, Teddy emerges victorious, though the antagonist ends up jailed and dies there.

Life is a memoir covering Keith Richards's life, starting with his childhood in Dartford, Kent, through to his success with the Rolling Stones and his current life in Connecticut. His interest in music was triggered by his mother, Doris, who played records by Sarah Vaughan, Billy Eckstine and Louis Armstrong, and his maternal grandfather, Augustus Theodore Dupree, a former big band player, who encouraged him to take up the guitar. In his teens he met up with Mick Jagger, who he had known in primary school, and discovered that they both shared a love of blues music. In the early 1960s Richards moved into a London flat, shared with Jagger and Brian Jones. Together with Bill Wyman, Ian Stewart and Charlie Watts, the Rolling Stones were founded in 1962, playing gigs at Ealing Jazz Club and the Crawdaddy Club. The book chronicles Richards's career with the Stones since 1962, following their rise from playing small club gigs to stadium concerts, Richards's drug habits, his arrests and convictions. His relationships with a number of women, including Anita Pallenberg, Marianne Faithfull, Ronnie Spector and Patti Hansen, whom he married in 1983, are covered in detail. The often difficult partnership between Richards and Jagger is referred to throughout the work and coverage of this has caused much media interest. Throughout the work, much attention is given to Richards' love of music, his style of playing and chord construction. His non-Stones projects, such as the X-Pensive Winos and recording with the Wingless Angels in Jamaica, as well as collaborations with Chuck Berry and Gram Parsons amongst others are covered in some detail.

The Wylies, a well-to-do but uneducated Scottish family, are concerned about their daughter, Maggie, a plain young woman who they fear, will remain a spinster. One night the Wylies discover that a serious young university student, John Shand, has been breaking into their home so that he can read books from their large library. Shand is penniless and cannot afford to buy books for his law school education. Maggie Wylie and John Shand come to an understanding: that her family will fund his education if, at the end of five years, he agrees to marry her. John honours his commitment to Maggie, marrying her although he does not love her. Recognising her husband's ambition to become a Member of Parliament, Maggie quietly uses her intelligence and her connections behind the scenes to get John elected. She continues to foster his career, never allowing him to see that she is the power behind his rise to fame. Eventually John begins to believe that his wife is too plain for a man of his stature and position, and he takes up with Lady Sybil Lazenby, a beautiful, refined and high-born young Englishwoman. Maggie is prepared to let her husband go, if Sybil can help him more than she herself can. However, when Shand is preparing a speech that will make or break his career, he finds that Sybil is no help to him, and he realises that Maggie is his inspiration.

The novel unfolds around a case of mistaken identity involving two identical twins, a scenario Jin Yong later notes evokes Shakespearean echoes such as Twelfth Night and The Comedy of Errors. The narrator-protagonist calls himself Gouzazhong, a term meaning “mongrel dog” or bastard, and begins as a penniless youth roaming Kaifeng in search of his lost mother. His path crosses a brawl among wulin fighters, where he encounters the Shi family and members of the Snowy Mountain Sect. An accident separates him from Kaifeng and places him under the care of a martial artist named Xie Yanke, who brings him to a secluded home atop Motian Cliff. There, Yanke, though frequently irritated by Gouzazhong, decides to mentor him in martial arts. For six years Gouzazhong trains in qi cultivation under Yanke’s guidance; what he does not realize is that Yanke harbors a hidden, malicious plan—teaching him the wrong methods to ensure internal wounds and eventual death. Meanwhile, Shi Potian, the leader of the Changle Sect (whose true name is Shi Zhongyu), vanishes without explanation. Much of the narrative follows the tangled consequences of Gouzhazhong’s mistaken identity: not only sect members with ulterior motives, but also Shi Zhongyu’s parents, his beloved Ding Dang, and the Snowy Mountain Sect all misrecognize him as Shi Zhongyu. Although the pair share striking resemblance, their dispositions are poles apart: Gouzhazhong remains straightforward, sincere, and quick-witted, whereas Shi Zhongyu is infamous for being lewd and calculating. Through these events, Gouzhazhong attains formidable martial prowess. Pursued by Snowy Mountain Sect adherents who suspect him of molesting A’xiu—the granddaughter of their sect leader—Gouzazhong ends up forming a relationship with A’xiu after a series of episodes in which misunderstandings are gradually resolved. The climax arrives when leaders from various factions are compelled to travel to a secluded island by two enigmatic, highly skilled messengers to partake in Laba congee for the festival. The tale then pivots toward a startling finale, offering revelations about Gouzhazhong’s true parentage and uncovering further secrets revealed on the island.

Though published as three volumes, the Deed of Paksenarrion was written as one continuous narrative. Some readers have highlighted parallels to Dungeons & Dragons: notably, Brewersbridge in Moon’s tale resembles Hommlet from The Temple of Elemental Evil, and the faith of Gird mirrors Saint Cuthbert’s worship in Greyhawk. Yet such motifs appear across many strands of high fantasy and are not exclusive to any single fictional universe. The tale centers on the adult life of Paksenarrion Dorthansdotter, nicknamed Paks, who hails from Three Firs. Set in a medieval-style realm inhabited by humans, dwarves, gnomes, and elves, the story opens with an 18-year-old Paks, headstrong and dissatisfied with an arranged marriage arranged by her father, who leaves Three Firs to enlist in a mercenary company. Through trials and travels she gradually discovers that she possesses paladin gifts, though in a way that deviates from conventional expectations.

In an Edinburgh squat, Detective Inspector John Rebus discovers a man’s body, an overdose victim laid out crosswise between two extinguished candles, a five-pointed star painted above on the wall. While some colleagues dismiss it as a routine junkie death, Rebus notes odd details that unsettle him: a complete heroin packet in the deceased’s room and peculiar bruising on his face and body. He treats the apparent murder as a real possibility and delves into the true circumstances behind the death. During his inquiry, Rebus encounters a young woman named Tracy, who knew the victim and heard his chilling last words: “Hide! Hide!” It turns out the man was a photographer who had snapped and concealed sensitive photographs at Hyde’s, a private club catering to an elite circle that also hosts illegal boxing. Rebus ultimately secures the arrest of Hyde’s proprietor and several prominent members, but, to his horror, they all die under dubious circumstances. The authorities are actively concealing the truth to avert a scandal. Soon after Rankin’s own relocation to London, a parallel real-world incident emerged: male prostitutes had bribed lawyers and judges. Parliament was prompted to investigate, and two lawyers began probing the police inquiry. In an unexpected turn, the inquiry concluded the allegations were unfounded, resulting in demotions for officers involved in the case.

Steven Masters, the main character, is a pampered 23-year-old and the sole heir to the planet’s wealthiest man. During a party, while intoxicated, he declares a desire to join a distant space mission bound for Mittend, a life-bearing world 30 light-years from Earth. When told he does not qualify, he reacts with indignation and launches a campaign to secure a seat on the expedition. Funds from his father enable him to obtain a berth, and six weeks later he lands on Mittend. The planet closely resembles Earth, boasting a breathable atmosphere. Once ashore, he strays from the group and encounters the indigenous people. They are naked and primitive but possess a collectivist intellect called “Mother.” As soon as they glimpse Steven, they pursue him; upon capturing and touching him, his consciousness is transferred into the body of a 38-year-old bar waiter back on Earth. In a twist, the bar waiter’s mind takes over Steven’s body on Mittend. It later emerges that the bar waiter had previously worked for Steven as a butler; he blames Steven for a crime he did not commit and got him fired. Right after the transfer, Steven experiences severe psychological shock, and the bar must call an ambulance. He spends several days hospitalized while doctors sedate him. News of his mind swap spreads, and the disappearance of the expedition amplifies the sensation surrounding his story. During his hospital stay, Masters Senior, his father, visits and later departs, insisting that the person lying in the hospital bed is not Steven. After leaving, a bartender arrives to pick him up and drive him to work, where he spends the day performing his duties.

The tale opens as Des Grieux, accompanied by his mother, attends a concert where he experiences uncanny, suggestive visions during a piano performance by the alluring Teleny, a Hungarian virtuoso. Drawn to him, Des Grieux becomes consumed by a mysterious, telepathic bond that seems both sexual and emotional, a mixture of fascination, admiration, and longing that soon morphs into jealousy. Aware that Teleny attracts many suitors before they become involved, Des Grieux and the elder musician finally meet and exchange accounts of their inexplicable connection, which quickly blossoms into an intense affair. Torn between love and desire for a man, Des Grieux briefly pursues a relationship with a household servant; this doomed pursuit indirectly precipitates the servant’s death. Shaken, he resolves to embrace his feelings and allows Teleny to introduce him to a clandestine circle of men drawn to other men’s desires. Their bond survives a coercive blackmail attempt and the emotional turmoil that follows, until Teleny announces a temporary departure, supposedly for a concert engagement. In this absence, Des Grieux visits Teleny’s apartment only to discover him in bed with Des Grieux’s mother, who had offered to settle Teleny’s debts in exchange for sexual favors. The scene shatters them, and Des Grieux sinks into despair, nearly ending his life in a hospital isolation. After his release, he seeks out Teleny, only to learn that his lover has stabbed himself in a gesture of remorse as he bleeds to death. Des Grieux forgives him; they reaffirm their love, but Teleny dies in the end.

Twelve-year-old Heidi resides in Reno, Nevada, living with her mentally challenged mother and their neighbor, Bernadette. Her mother speaks only twenty-three words, one of which remains a mystery—“soof”—a term no one can define. Bernadette, meanwhile, suffers from severe agoraphobia and dares not venture outside. To provide for everyone, Heidi shoulders responsibilities far beyond her years. When she uncovers photographs of her mother at a Christmas party in New York, Heidi resolves to travel there, driven by a desire to learn more about her family’s past and to uncover the meaning of the circulating word—soof—after hearing her mother mutter it repeatedly. Bernadette, anxious about Heidi’s departure, grants permission only if she promises to phone every night. On her journey to Liberty, New York, Heidi befriends Georgia Sweet, a warm and inquisitive woman she meets aboard the bus. Upon arriving at Hilltop Home, Heidi feels unwelcome in Thurman Hill’s presence. Overcome with sadness, Ruby welcomes Heidi into her own home and, with her husband Roy, begins to investigate. Through their sleuthing, Heidi discovers Thurman Hill is her grandfather, Elliot is her father, and her grandmother’s name is Diana. She finally learns the true meaning of her mother’s enigmatic word—soof—which turns out to be Heidi’s nickname for Sophia Demuth. The story closes with the death of Heidi’s mother.

In the prologue, Watarai leads his squad, the Cobalt Knights, into a zone barred to ordinary players. They attempt to erase a stray AI resembling a young girl in a red dress, but their effort fails and she escapes. Chapter one introduces Albireo, who sneaks into the dungeon’s lowest floor and encounters the Vagrant AI. Via text chat, she reveals her name as Lycoris. The dungeon’s final treasure is an item labeled “eciov.cyl,” which Albiero trades to Lycoris at her request. Within the game, Lycoris gains a voice. She then teleports them without warning to Albireo’s home, where a massive monster outbreak is underway. A novice player named Hokuto pleads with Albireo for help; he must assist, compelled by circumstance, and receives an item named “rae.cyl,” which is also given to Lycoris. Hokuto manipulates Albireo into allowing her onto his empty friends list and eventually into forming a two-person party. This arrangement lets Hokuto see Lycoris. Orca and Balmung later approach Albireo, asking him to join the effort to resolve the “One Sin,” a supposedly unbeatable event, but he declines. Although he cannot log out of The World, he continues his real life as usual, unlike later .hack characters who fall into comas. Returning to the “One Sin” location, Albireo reunites with Hokuto there, witnessing Orca and Balmung defeat the boss. After its fall, an angel appears, its body trailing feathers. Lycoris asks Albireo to locate a red feather, which turns out to be “eye.cyl,” restoring her sight. Lycoris then escorts them to another zone, where she enters a phantom spring and Albireo acquires “yromem.cyl.” Back in the prologue area, Albireo gives Lycoris the item, enabling her to recover her memories and recognize Albireo as Watarai, the Cobalt Knight who first attempted to delete her. Watarai had aimed to complete the event to erase the previously fragmented Lycoris. Lycoris informs him of Morganna Mode Gone and of her origin as a failed Aura prototype, revealing the final fragment of herself stored in Albireo’s spear: “etaf.cyl.” In the end, she chooses to delete herself, stabbing herself onto Albireo’s spear.

Dalgliesh undertakes a semi-official visit to Saint Anselm’s to review a student’s death that occurred some time earlier, prompted by the father’s dissatisfaction with the verdict. While there, a visiting Archdeacon is killed, and Dalgliesh takes charge of the ensuing inquiry, enlisting support from London detectives Miskin and Tarrant in addition to local officers. Early leads point to a college father who runs and teaches there, since the archdeacon had been urging the institution’s closure. As the investigation unfolds, two more murders occur. After questioning everyone present, a series of hidden truths comes to light: one student is unknowingly the son of a lay lecturer, and through his mother he stands to inherit the college’s assets if it is ever shut and sold. Forensic analysis seals the lecturer’s guilt, and he admits to the crime. The college is subsequently closed, with the inheritance passing to the student. Amid these events, Dalgliesh begins a romance with Dr Emma Lavenham, a visiting lecturer from Cambridge.

The narrative begins in autumn 1558, soon after Mary I’s death, with bells announcing that Elizabeth, Mary’s half-sister, has ascended to the throne. The tale unfolds through four principal viewpoints: Elizabeth I herself, her chief advisor William Cecil, Robert Dudley—Elizabeth’s favored confidant—and Amy Robsart, Dudley’s wife. Dudley returns to court at Elizabeth’s coronation, while Amy hopes his ambitions won’t jeopardize him. Under Mary’s reign, Dudley spent time in the Tower of London; his father and brother were executed, and another brother perished in Calais. Yet Amy’s optimism for a tranquil life proves short-lived as Elizabeth and Dudley grow nearer and more intimate. Elizabeth inherits a bankrupt, discontented realm already unsettled by the precedents set by the two previous monarchs. Cecil warns that Elizabeth’s survival hinges on marrying a powerful prince, yet her heart longs for her childhood friend—now a married man—Robert Dudley. Dudley believes he can reclaim his fate by standing beside Elizabeth. As the queen and her courtier fall in love, Dudley begins to confront a nearly impossible idea: abandoning his wife to wed the young queen.

Five centuries after Earthfall’s end, Harmony’s lone original colonist remains: Shedemei, now donning the Cloak of the Starmaster, a conduit to the Oversoul. Centuries pass, and Nafai and Elemak’s lineages have built cities and towns, yet the old feud between the brothers lingers unforgotten. Yet the Oversoul still has not fulfilled its mission: locating the Keeper of Earth, the central intelligence capable of repairing the damaged counterpart at Harmony. The Keeper’s influence resumes spreading, and following the dreams, Shedemei chooses to return to Earth.
