This final Homecoming volume shifts away from the style and plot of the preceding four installments. All prior characters except Shedemei lie dead. The old Nafai–Elemak rivalry persists through their descendants, but it plays a secondary role here. The narrative centers on the struggles of Nafai’s followers’ descendants. Leading the action are the king of Darakemba, the empire founded by the Nafaris, his offspring and advisers, and the high priest of Darakemba with his progeny and converts, who drive the principal events of the tale.

Algarve renews an assault in the south of Unkerlant toward the Mamming Hills, which is Unkerlant's source of cinnabar, leading to the mammoth Battle of Sulingen. Kaunian refugees begin showing up in Zuwayza, which takes them in; other Kaunians get away from a caravan in Valmiera and come to the attention of Skarnu and his friends (who had blown up the caravan to disrupt the Algarvians) or are set loose in a Lagoan raid on a camp in Valmiera. Leofsig is killed by Sidroc, who joins the Plegmund's Brigade. Istvan and his squad accidentally eat goat stew in a raid on a camp in Unkerlant's western forest and are purified by their captain. The Algarvians kill Kaunians in the Land of the Ice People in an attempt to use magic against the Lagoans, but the magic from the killed Kaunians slaughters the Algarvian army instead, and Algarve is forced to withdraw from the continent completely, leaving it to the Lagoans. The wear on the Algarvians is showing as they start to rely more on Sibians, Forthwegians, and the unreliable Yaninans to keep up the fight against Unkerlant. The Battle of Sulingen is won by the Unkerlanters that winter, with Trasone dying in the very last scene in the book. Algarve is on the way to losing the war. The Naantali Project starts, and the Kuusamans take Obuda.

Blair Maynard, a divorced journalist in New York City, decides to write a story about the unexplained disappearance of yachts and other small boats in the Caribbean, hoping to debunk theories about the Bermuda Triangle. He has weekend custody of his preteen son Justin, and decides to mix a vacation with work, taking his son along. They fly from Miami to the Turks and Caicos island chain but, while on fishing trip, are captured by a band of pirates. The pirates have, amazingly, remained undetected since the establishment of their pirate enclave by Jean-David Nau, the notorious buccaneer L'Olonnais, in 1671 (in reality, however, L'Olonnais is known to have died four years earlier). The pirates have a constitution of sorts, called the Covenant, and have a cruel but workable society. They raise any children they capture to ensure the survival of the colony, but kill anyone over the age of thirteen. In short order, Justin is virtually brainwashed and groomed to lead the pirate band, much to Maynard's horror. Maynard tries repeatedly to escape, and finally attracts the attention of the passing United States Coast Guard cutter New Hope. The pirates attack and capture it, but Maynard is able to use a machine gun aboard to kill most of the pirates and to win Justin's and his own freedom.

During a post-concert cleanup in Yorkshire in 1969, volunteers uncover a young woman’s corpse wrapped in a sleeping bag, brutally slain. The case is assigned to Detective Stanley Chadwick, a hardened Second World War veteran whose rigid, conventional outlook clashes with the era’s rebellious, long-haired hippies, their marijuana, and the thrum of rock and roll. Determined to solve the murder, Chadwick suspects the victim had ties to the rising psychedelic folk-tinged group, the Mad Hatters. In the present day, Inspector Alan Banks probes the killing of a freelance music journalist who was writing a feature on the Mad Hatters for MOJO magazine. This isn’t the first brush with tragedy for the band, now aging rock icons; Banks must root through history to uncover the hornet’s nest provoked by the journalist’s report and how it all connects to the murder.”

The tale centers on Vikraman, the son of a fictional Chola king named Parthiban, and his attempt to throw off Pallava suzerainty under Narasimhavarman. The Cholas are portrayed as vassals, yearning to reclaim the bygone imperial glory that they believe has faded with their loss of sovereignty. Parthiban passes this longing to Vikraman, urging him to restore the dynasty’s former prominence. Refusing Pallava taxes triggers a Pallava assault on the Cholas. In the ensuing conflict, Parthiban falls, and a mysterious monk on the battlefield vows to ensure Vikraman fulfills his father’s dream. As time passes, Vikraman matures with plans to strike back at Narasimhavarman. His uncle, Marappa Bhupathi, betrays him, leading to Vikraman’s arrest and exile from India by the Pallavas. The narrative then follows his return, driven by a desire to reunite with his mother and the enigmatic beauty he had glimpsed before exile. Tragically, he learns his mother has vanished—indeed kidnapped by the ruthless Kapalikas, a tribe practicing human sacrifice. He also discovers that Kundhavi, the woman he loves, is the daughter of his arch-enemy Narasimhavarman. The climax reveals the monk’s true identity as the Pallava king Narasimhavarman and marks the establishment of an independent Chola realm under Vikraman at Uraiyur. In the finale, Vikraman weds Kundhavi.

Pauline Hannum, a strikingly young and beautiful daughter of the recently deceased Major Hannum, who also appears as a performer in his circus, visits The Magic Shop owned by The Great Merlini. She shows an unusually high willingness to pay well above the normal price to receive a “Headless Lady” illusion instantly. Moved by Merlini’s fascination with circuses, Merlini and his writer friend Ross Harte embark on an inquiry into her demand. Their investigation quickly uncovers evidence that Major Hannum’s death was likely murder, and that the culprit may still have urgent, dangerous business tied to a real headless lady whose head has vanished. Joined by a new ally, detective-writer Stuart Towne, Merlini and Harte uncover a raft of revealing backstage details about the circus world—such as why the orchestra’s playing of Suppé’s Light Cavalry March is considered bad luck, what the mummified remains of John Wilkes Booth are made of, and a method for forging fingerprints without loops or whorls. To solve the case, Merlini must wield his magical prowess to break out of an apparently escape-proof jail, gather the suspects, and disclose the murderer in a climactic, twist-filled finale.”

The vast lake, Lake Agassiz, covered much of North Dakota, Manitoba and Minnesota during prehistoric times. The story begins when farmer Tom Lasker and his son, Will, uncover a seemingly brand new yacht. Found on a landlocked farm, it draws tourists to the area. Max Collingswood, a friend of Tom's, tries to help discover the origins of the boat. Collingswood enlists April Cannon, a worker at a chemical lab who discovers that the yacht is made of an unknown material. In fact, it is a fiberglass-like material with an impossible atomic number (161). Collingswood and Cannon discover something else on a nearby ridge which is part of a Sioux reservation. The Sioux assist in its excavation and examination. It turns out to a green glassy roundhouse-like structure, made from the same material. Eventually, they gain access to it, revealing a dock for the sailboat, but no entrance for it. The discovery that the structure contains the means to access other sites not on Earth sets off a struggle between the Government and the Reservation for control of it.

In Calcutta, Protima, Inspector Ghote’s wife, has inherited wealth and a grand house, a development that unsettles Ghote because it forces him to abandon Mumbai and leave policing behind. Soon after arriving, the couple finds their new residence dilapidated and besieged by hostile squatters. A nearby wetlands area is slated for a housing project, and it happens to provide the only access route to the proposed development. Their solicitor, A. K. Dutt-Daster, who manages the will, urges a quick sale and a return to their former life, but Ghote suspects there is corruption at play. His inquiry uncovers a sprawling network of graft that climbs the social and political ladder of Calcutta. Along the way, he engages with a clerk who, though easily bribable, becomes a liability after he acquires incriminating documents from Dutt-Daster’s files and is murdered. Ghote is assaulted beneath The Great Banyan tree in the Indian Botanical Gardens, and crosses paths with a crusading newspaper editor who chooses his battles with care, a hardened and corrupt police inspector, and a powerful businessman who views bribery as acceptable. The odds—anchored by influential adversaries—press in from all sides, and the elderly couple’s position looks increasingly untenable. In the end, Ghote is compelled to pay a substantial bribe to ensure their escape from Calcutta with their freedom and lives. As he contemplates the inevitability of corruption and bribery in life, Ghote contends that such realities do not justify surrendering to them.

The book harshly critiques Richard Fuld, Henry Paulson, and the Gramm–Leach–Bliley Act of 1999, the Congressional measure signed by Bill Clinton that repealed parts of the Glass–Steagall Act of 1933. It recounts how, after completing his studies at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, McDonald sold pork chops, taught himself the material needed to pass the General Securities Representative Exam, and then built ConvertBond.com, a site eventually acquired by Morgan Stanley. The author credits his expertise in the convertible-bond market as the driving force behind launching ConvertBond.com during the dot-com boom and his successful sale to Morgan Stanley before the market bubble burst. While employed at Morgan Stanley, McDonald received an offer to serve as vice president at Lehman Brothers. The narration depicts Richard Fuld as detached, arrogant, and a harsh, hot-tempered, ruthless chief executive with a tendency toward anger, whom the book mockingly labels as “his majesty,” “god-like,” and a “spiritual leader.” McDonald contends that the U.S. government should have rescued Lehman Brothers, and that Fuld wrongly assumed federal intervention would come after a spring 2008 meeting with Henry Paulson, a miscalculation that spurred him to take on unnecessary risk and to reject an $18-per-share proposal from the Korea Development Bank as late as August 2008.

A psychiatric patient, having wandered off course, finds himself in the land of Kappa. There, he is welcomed as a distinguished guest and engages in conversations with Kappas from various professions. Geeru, a radical capitalist, declares that Kappa’s unemployed workers are slain and their flesh is repurposed as sustenance. The patient is stunned, yet Geeru argues that the patient’s objections are merely sentimental, noting that the poorest Japanese women are forced into prostitution simply to survive. Kappa’s national character is framed as a blend of materialism and nihilistic realism, and the babies of Kappa supposedly determine their own fates. In the womb, a fetus may reject life as a Kappa and be aborted. The Maggu—an introspective Kappa who commits suicide—haunts the living as a ghost inhabiting Tokku, a poet. Maggu worries about posthumous fame, even as he admires writers and philosophers who died by suicide, such as Heinrich von Kleist and Otto Weininger. Eventually the patient is set to return to the human world, but he reflects that Kappa remains pristine and superior to human society, leading him to become misanthropic.

The story concerns Lancelot who has survived to the present day by means of magic. He must help Morgana le Fay confront Merlin, who is half-mad and attempting to meddle in the affairs of the world. Lancelot has remained alive since the fall of Camelot, having the appearance of an elderly man but retaining his strength and fighting skills. He has spent his long life seeking the Holy Grail, believing that his immortality is punishment for his sins, and that finding the Grail will end his curse. Lancelot instead learns from Morgana le Fay that Merlin is responsible for his condition. Merlin has slept for centuries, but is about to awaken, and intends for Lancelot to be his champion and protector. Morgana warns Lancelot that Merlin will cause great harm in his misguided attempts to right the wrongs of the modern world, and that he must be stopped. Lancelot finds Merlin and rejuvenates him from his centuries-long sleep with a magic elixir. Lancelot tries to persuade Merlin to desist from his plans, and Merlin removes the spell of immortality. Anticipating Merlin, Lancelot drinks the remainder of the elixir to restore his own youth. Merlin summons a "hollow knight" (a suit of armor animated by a spirit) to kill Lancelot. Morgana defeats Merlin, and Lancelot vanquishes the spirit, but is mortally wounded. As Lancelot dies, he finally sees a vision of the Holy Grail.

Democracy in America centers on explaining why republican representative government has thrived in the United States yet faltered in numerous other contexts. Tocqueville aims to transpose the functional strengths of American democracy onto the perceived shortcomings of democracy in his homeland, France. He then speculates about the future trajectory of American democracy, outlining potential threats and perils it may face. Among these concerns are his warnings that democracy can slide into “soft despotism” and that a tyranny of the majority could emerge. He notes that religion assumes a robust, influential role in the United States precisely because it remains separate from government—a separation that all political factions endorse. By contrast, he sees in France a corrosive tension between democrats and religion, a tension he links to the intertwining of church and state. In Volume II, Tocqueville enriches his political analysis with a portrayal of civil society as a realm of private and nonstate life. His outlook on America darkens after 1840, a shift that is documented by Aurelian Craiutu in Tocqueville on America after 1840: Letters and Other Writings.”

At the outset, Tamis, a sorceress, gazes into the future and realizes that only a mixed-blood Spartan named Parmenion can assist her. Parmenion—a half-blood Spartan whose mother hails from Macedon—is a gifted runner and a strategic mind, yet he is scorned by the young Spartan nobles. After killing a rival in a duel to defend a love, he is forced to flee to Thebes. There he begins a new life as a professional runner and becomes entangled with Theban rebels seeking to dislodge the Spartan garrison entrenched in the city’s heart. This involvement sparks a protracted war between the two polities, culminating in Parmenion’s decisive rout of the Spartan army and the destruction of the Spartan legend. Years later, he has become a celebrated mercenary general, earning victories across Asia. He then receives an invitation to help rebuild the Macedonian army under Philip II of Macedon. The tale subsequently traces the rise of Macedon under Philip II and the birth of Alexander the Great. fr:Le Lion de Macédoine pl:Lew Macedonii

The narrative centers on Josef, a grandfather who recounts events in the first person. After returning from Soviet captivity at war’s end, he discovers his wife Katharina entangled in an affair. Throughout the tale, he pursues reconciliation with her, and his efforts bear fruit as she descends into madness and increasingly seeks him out. The lineage unfolds across generations, exposing strained, damaged souls and a string of murders, including his son’s death by suicide. A pivotal moment reveals Josef’s wartime order to execute a Russian commissar, carried out under the grim, punitive logic of the Commissar Order, without room for mercy. In a needless act, he then kills another crouching figure who is already dead. Later, Katharina’s mental turmoil is explained: the “visitors” she imagines inhabiting their apartment are really deceased family members. They reappear in the narrative as a quasi-ghostly troupe on a fictional plane, while the living protagonists seem to be real. The reader discerns this reversal as the actual kin begin to die. In the conclusion, the storyteller’s perspective shifts to reveal that the narrator himself is, in truth, the spirits of the slain boys.

The book opens with Richard Bolitho arriving at an inn frequented by Midshipmen in Portsmouth. There he meets another midshipman Martyn Dancer. They are retrieved by a lieutenant from the Gorgon. The ship sails towards West Africa, where they encounter an empty Merchantman, the City of Athens. Dancer and Bolitho are sent aboard the ship, and discover that the ship has been pillaged and the crew killed. The officers soon deduce that the ship was raided by Pirates and Captain Conway announces that the Admiralty had dispatched them to investigate the disappearance of ships in the region. In company with the captured City of Athens, the Gorgon approaches a coastal fort surrounded by treacherous reefs and shoals. Upon approaching the fort, they see that two ships are in the nearby harbour, however the fort opens fire and destroys the City of Athens. The Gorgon withdraws and returns during the dark of the night to cut out the ship. Dancer and Bolitho are sent on the mission, commanded by the 4th lieutenant, Mr. Tregorren, who holds a grudge and mistreats Bolitho over Bolitho's prestigious heritage. They succeed at taking the ship, and also capture a Slave Dhow in the escape with the help of the Gorgon. The ships, under the guise at being members of the pilot fleet raid the castle from which the pirates had been using as a base.

Summer settles over Lake Eden, Minnesota, and excitement runs high for the family reunion that Hannah’s partner, Lisa, has organized. Unexpectedly, Uncle Gus returns after a thirty-year absence, arriving with lavish jewelry, stylish outfits, and a new car, instantly becoming the focal point of the gathering. The responsibility of supplying the treats falls to Hannah Swensen, owner of The Cookie Jar bakery, who serves up one of her specialties—carrot cake—that proves especially popular. Gus admires the cake and requests another tray, but the next day, during the family reunion photo session, one person is conspicuously missing. Hannah searches for Gus and discovers him at the pavilion bar, near two pieces of carrot cake, dead from an ice-pick stabbing. The mystery falls squarely on Hannah to unravel. With Grandpa Jack showing signs of Alzheimer’s, suspicion initially points toward him as the killer, but Hannah believes he is innocent and sets out to clear him. The story also includes recipes.

When people and dogs vanish suddenly and eerie screams pierce the night, the notion of vengeful spirits begins to seem plausible. These peculiar events draw Frank and Joe Hardy to the Pocono Mountains to assist their father’s friend, a retired police captain, in unraveling the mystery of Black Hollow. Upon reaching Captain Thomas Maguire’s cabin at the hollow’s rim with Chet Morton, they learn he has vanished. In the surrounding woods, only scant clues remain: a flashlight stamped with the initials T.M., scraps of bright plaid fabric, and two freshly fired shotgun shells. Despite Chet’s warnings after a night of unnerving, terrifying cries, the brothers resolve to locate the captain. Neighbors insist the bloodcurdling sounds belong to a legendary witch haunting Black Hollow in pursuit of vengeance. In a twist, it is a small puppy that helps the boys uncover an unusual and startling chain of events, linking a mute boy, a reclusive hermit, and a fearless trainer of pumas.

Told through the perspectives of the novel’s central figures, the narrative centers on Jacob Hunt, an eighteen-year-old with Asperger’s syndrome, a high-functioning form of autism. He lives with his mother and brother, Emma and Theo Hunt, and thrives only when daily routines are meticulously planned; any disruption or surprise unsettles him. His fixation on forensic analysis dominates his life, shaping much of the plot. The story begins with Jacob arranging a staged crime scene for his mother to investigate, effectively making himself the victim of the scenario. His relentless attention to detail and need for structure frequently exhaust Emma and provoke Theo’s anger. When counselor Jess Ogilvy, who helps Jacob navigate social situations, is found dead, suspicion quickly falls on him. After the first suspect, Mark Maguire, is detained and released, Detective Rich Matson requests Emma’s permission to interview Jacob. Following Jacob’s confession that he moved Jess’s corpse, he is arrested and charged with murder, and the case moves to trial. During proceedings, prosecutor Helen Sharp emphasizes how closely Jacob’s Asperger’s symptoms resemble traits often associated with guilt, challenging the reliability of behavioral cues. The prosecution also points to physical and documentary evidence they claim links Jacob to the crime—his fingerprints at the scene, a crime-scene evaluation in his notebook that mirrors Jess’s, and a backpack belonging to Jess retrieved from her home. On the witness stand, Jacob claims that he found Jess dead in her bathroom, bleeding from a head wound. He admits to having cleaned Jess, dressing her, and moving her outside, then tidying the original crime scene and fabricating a fresh one intended to mislead investigators. He explains this was driven by the realization that the death, though it began as an accident, resulted from Theo’s presence in the house and an encounter with Jess; after witnessing her naked in the shower, Theo fled, and Jess slipped and died. In the end, the court accepts that Jess’s death was indeed an accident, resolving the case as a fatal mishap rather than a deliberate murder."

Arthur Zouch, a portrait painter who dubs himself a “superman,” arrives at Passenger Court ostensibly to paint Mary, the younger Passenger daughter. Yet his visit is driven as much by a hunger for social advancement, financial gain, and sexual satisfaction as by artistic purpose. At the manor, he discovers openings for all three motives, but encounters unforeseen resistance in Vernon Passenger—another self-styled “superman”—who stands in his way. Nearby, the Fosdicks—the Major and his sons, Torquil and Jasper—maintain a long-running feud with the Passengers. Their quarrels are as likely to be tempered by superior manners and proper etiquette as by fiery tempers and sharp disputes. A local young woman named Joanna Brandon adds further complication to several characters’ lives; Powell’s portrayal of her is perhaps the novel’s most delicately drawn female figure. Spanning ten chapters, the narrative builds toward an unavoidable denouement, even as it withholds the exact means by which the book’s title foreshadowing will come to pass. The intertwined plots—sometimes reminiscent of Lear’s arc for the neighboring clans—converge on a double climax, from which only one self-styled “superman” can emerge.

Guadalupe "Lupe" Guardado is a middle-aged Salvadoran woman who lives near Chalatenango, El Salvador. During the day she is required to do what she can to support her family, while her husband works for a wealthy landowner. Her husband José has become involved in rebellion against the economic conditions and became a leader in the Christian farmers organization. Fearing persecution for his opposition, José regularly stays "in the hills" after work and sees his family little. The Guardado's son Justino was killed by the "authorities" prior to the events in the novel, and their son-in-law Helio has "disappeared." Guadalupe's granddaughter Adolfina relays the protest at a cathedral, as well as a massacre of students on a bus. At the end of the novel, the authorities bring a beaten man to Guadalupe and Adolfina who had said the name "Adolfina" after being severely beaten. Adolfina does not recognize the man, but Guadalupe recognizes her husband José. On his previous advice, she denies knowing him, and he is taken away.

Joseph and Harriet Blackstone, and Joseph's mother Lilian, are immigrants from England on the SS Albert into the South Island of New Zealand in 1860s. After settling the two women into accommodation in Christchurch, Joseph travels to the foothills near the Okuku river to build their Cob House. Joseph returns to Christchurch once the house has been built and the three of them set off to start their new lives on their farm. The harsh first winter brings with it problems which threaten the viability of their farm, but Joseph's chance finding of gold in the nearby creek changes the situation. Not telling Harriet about the find, Joseph abandons the farm and travels by boat to Hokitika on the West Coast of the South Island where major gold strikes have occurred. After Lilian's death, Harriet also travels to Hokitika and delivers that news to Joseph. The search for gold, the 'colour', goes on in difficult conditions. Joseph's encounters with Will Sefton, a young man whom he met on the boat bringing them to the West Coast, and Pao Yi, a Chinese gardener befriended by Harriet, add flavour to the dynamics of the searching couple's relationship which has become distant and strained. Joseph's guilt surrounding events in England prior to their emigration impact on this separation.

The events of Homeboyz takes place four to five years after the events in Hip Hop High School. The book's main character is 17-year-old Dixon Theodore Anderson, nicknamed Teddy. He is a smart teenager who is both a hacker and a bodybuilder. Teddy's entire neighborhood is overrun by gangsters and his sister, Tina Anderson, is killed in a crossfire. While the Anderson family mourns her death, Teddy goes to his car to seek vengeance. He is unsuccessful in getting revenge and is arrested. He then spends time in a California juvenile prison waiting for a judge to hear his case. During this time, Teddy is treated as if he was a gangster. He is set free, but is put under house arrest and is enrolled in a probation program. Teddy is forced to spend five days each week mentoring a kid named Micah. Teddy has difficulty tutoring Micah because he is wants to be a gangster. But through Micah, teddy is taught how to love someone and see how people can change. Also this book talks about when Teddy meets the person that killed his sister,and he wasn't from 0-1-0. He was a member of another rival gang. Teddy fought hard and he won but the guy was sent to jail and died there.

This book takes a 'warts and all' sensible yet humorous look at the many stages of pregnancy. It explores the changes, physical and emotional, that any man can expect to see in his partner and in their relationship over the coming months. Becoming pregnant involved two people. The rearing of a child will involve two people; there is every reason that your partner's pregnancy should also involve the two of you, together. For any man that has been put off reading pregnancy books because he doesn't feel he was the intended audience or that something about the tone of these books was alien to him, yet he still has questions that need answers; then The Blokes' Guide to: Pregnancy is the book he's been looking for. As a father himself, Jon Smith realized, when his partner Lisa became pregnant that there was nothing out there that he could relate to. The Bloke's Guide to Pregnancy is the result. Jon takes a comical yet informed look at the ups and downs of life as a father to be. Guaranteed to educate you while making you laugh out loud!

Set in the town of Bolton, South Dakota, Reacher begins his latest adventure on a wrecked senior citizen tour bus after a near-miss with another motorist leaves the bus spinning on the icy road and trapped in a snowy bank. Immersed in a snowy, frozen landscape, Reacher works with local law enforcement to help the fragile victims. Hours later, Reacher learns Bolton is not like most towns. Beside its freezing, snowy climate, the town plays host to one of the largest prisons in the U.S., making the town and its law enforcement subject to the needs and demands of the gigantic correctional facility. At the same time, a band of outlaw bikers, settled outside the town, are on edge after their leader is arrested on drug charges. As the biker awaits trial, protecting Janet Salter, the only witness to the biker's drug transaction, becomes a top priority, and Reacher agrees to aid local law enforcement to help protect the elderly Salter. Throughout the story, brutal enemies, both foreign and domestic, are encountered. The foreign criminal from Mexico is named Plato, and the bad cop in Bolton is Chief Holland, who murders his deputy chief, Andrew Peterson; a crooked lawyer; and the witness Salter. Reacher finds help from one of his successors, Susan Turner, the current leader of the elite 110th Special Investigations Unit (Reacher's old command), while interesting new details of his past come to light, such as how a dent appeared in his desk (from injuring a corrupt general), and of how Reacher caught the attention of military command because of his childhood behavior patterns. The ending leaves the reader guessing as to the conclusion. We do not learn how Reacher manages to escape an underground facility filled with fuel by Plato's henchmen before it ignites. A brief description of how he survives the conflagration appears in the next Reacher novel, Worth Dying For.

In Santa Barbara, California, the tale unfolds as Travis Cornell—an ex-Delta Force operative—questions the point of his life while wandering a nearby canyon. There he meets two escaped specimens from a secret government lab: a golden retriever endowed with extraordinary intellect that quickly befriends him, and a menacing creature called the Outsider that seems bent on hurting the dog. After escaping the pursuing Outsider, Travis brings the dog home and christens him Einstein. Parallel to this, Nora Devon, a shy young woman who has recently lost an abusive aunt, is assaulted in her residence by a man attempting a rape. Travis and Einstein intervene, and a strong bond soon forms among the trio. Before long, Travis, Nora, and Einstein are forced to flee—not only from the menacing Outsider but also from federal agents intent on recapturing the lab fugitives, and from Vince Nasco, a remorseless assassin hired to eliminate the creatures and silence any witnesses who cross his path.

Kristien, a white academic narrator, returns to South Africa to visit her grandmother after an assault by black youths leaves the old woman bedridden. Before she dies, the grandmother hopes to share the story of their Afrikaner lineage, a mission both women deem crucial. Kristien’s memories of life in London reveal a period of aimlessness and passivity, during which she sought distance from South Africa and from parents who, in life, supported apartheid. Initially, relinquishing her self-imposed exile feels like mere resignation, but gradually she recognizes that her homeland is evolving for the better. With the first democratic elections approaching, Kristien meets both black and white people, and the grandmother’s tales—framing largely the female line and tracing back to a black matriarch—teach Kristien to claim South Africa as her homeland. On the eve of the vote, Kristien’s sister murders her own children and her violent, racist husband, then takes her own life to escape an unbearable existence. That same night, the grandmother dies from injuries sustained in the assault. Yet Kristien remains hopeful about her future in South Africa. The family farm is bequeathed to the household of the black domestic worker.

Set in contemporary West Virginia, the story follows Summer, an orphaned girl passed from one indifferent relative to the next. At six, she meets Aunt May and Uncle Ob, a kindly elderly pair who notice that Summer is not abused but largely overlooked. They bring her into their creaky hillside trailer, and for the first time she senses a real, stable home. Six years later, Aunt May dies suddenly in the garden, leaving Summer to wrestle with grief while witnessing Uncle Ob’s struggle with living after her loss. In his despair, he turns to spirit contact, spurred by a sensation that May is trying to reach him. He is aided by Cletus Underwood, a classmate of Summer who knows of a famed medium. Although skeptical, Summer is willing to explore any path that might ease her uncle’s sorrow. The trio embarks on a road trip to consult the medium, only to learn she has recently passed away. Uncle Ob’s initial heartbreak threatens to extinguish his will to live, but a turn of hope comes on the return journey as he chooses to keep carrying on for Summer’s sake.

It's a winter day in Dalton (a New England town near Boston) and Leonidas Witherall, "the man who looks like Shakespeare", is returning to his new house, which he's never seen. He's inherited money from an uncle and toured the world, and left plans for his home to be built while on his travels, but now he must return home and produce the next volume of the adventures of Lieutenant Haseltine. On the train to Dalton, he meets a mousy woman named Miss Chard (known to all as Swiss Chard) and a beautiful young woman with a brown paper package and a secret. His new home proves a delight, and it includes a kitchen filled with red appliances, a library with ladders, and a garage complete with the pickaxed corpse of Medora, the crabby next-door neighbor. Leonidas assembles a gang of assistants, including dotty housewife Cassie Price and former car thief Cuff (who has reformed and joined the police force). Together, they defend Witherall's new red refrigerator against thieves, track down the missing envelope of money and bring the murderer to justice.

Albert, a 42-year-old still living in his father’s apartment in Harstad, faces his father’s sudden death as a chance to finally craft the life he’s longed for during years of caregiving. Much of the narrative unfolds through a flashback to 1985–86, detailing his European travels with a friend named Viktor, a stop in Hong Kong by sheer happenstance, and a later sojourn in Paris where he meets a girl and nearly chooses to stay, only to return to Hässelby to be with his father. What begins as a conventional exploration of father–son dynamics, suburban upbringing, friendship, and political currents gradually darkens as increasingly surreal imagery intrudes. The ending shifts into a nightmare: Albert learns that someone has been shadowing him for more than two decades across continents, and that the world itself is on the brink of collapse.

Tommy Segovia, Calder’s old friend who had left town a year earlier, has returned to Hyde Park in Chicago—and immediately feels envious of Calder and Petra, who earned the figurative “glory” of saving a Vermeer in the previous book, Chasing Vermeer. He believes he deserves a share of that recognition. On the first day of the new term, Ms. Hussey reveals that the world-famous Robie House is slated for demolition, calling it an act of murder. The class then tours the house, where Calder and Petra uncover a web of concealed truths about the building. After Tommy learns to tolerate Petra, the trio—calling themselves The Wright 3—band together to protect the house, even breaking in near the end. During their adventures, Tommy discovers a fish talisman in the Robie House garden and realizes its high value. In the end, after fending off burglars inside the Robie House, they succeed in preserving both themselves and the landmark. Throughout the drawings, a fish motif—referencing Frank Lloyd Wright’s lucky talisman—appears in nearly every illustration, often hidden by nature and aligned with the Fibonacci sequence in each chapter. One of the final illustrations even hides a dragon, signaling a shift from carp to dragon in the narrative. Near the bottom of the last image, footprints suggest the presence of the invisible man, and several pictures reveal a face if you look closely.

In Venice, Volpone—an affluent gentleman—fakes a terminal illness to dupe three would-be heirs: Voltore, Corbaccio, and Corvino, all eager for his wealth. Each arrives bearing lavish gifts, hoping to be named heir in Volpone’s will. Mosca, Volpone’s scheming parasite, engineers the illusion, convincing every suitor that the others have been disinherited in favor of Volpone, and even persuades Corbaccio to cut his own son out of the will. He also informs Volpone that Corvino possesses a beautiful wife, Celia. Disguised as Scoto the Mountebank, Volpone visits Celia; though Corvino drives him away, Volpone’s fixation on Celia only grows. Mosca then insinuates that Volpone’s recovery requires sexual indulgence with a young woman, prompting Corvino to offer Celia to please Volpone. Just as Corvino and Celia are due to arrive for this arrangement, Bonario—Corbaccio’s son—appears, intent on exposing his father’s disinheritance scheme. Mosca steers him into a side chamber while Volpone remains with Celia; after failing to win her over with luxury fantasies, Volpone attempts to rape her. Bonario intervenes to rescue Celia. The ensuing courtroom confrontation is carefully impounded by Mosca, Volpone, and the three deceived heirs, who manage to bury the truth. The play also features episodes with the English travelers Sir and Lady Politick Would-Be and Peregrine. Sir Politic constantly harbors grandiose plots and schemes, while Lady Would-Be tests Volpone with incessant chatter. Mosca orchestrates a mistaken liaison between them, leaving Peregrine—more perceptive than the others—feeling slighted. He shames Sir Politick by announcing his arrest for sedition, forcing him to hide inside a giant tortoise shell. Volpone, too, urges concealment and the pretense that he has died, bequeathing his fortune to Mosca. This provokes Voltore, Corbaccio, and Corvino to fury, and the entire company returns to court. Volpone becomes entangled in the web of schemes he and Mosca devised. Although he pleads, Mosca refuses to relinquish his newly acquired wealth, and Volpone resolves to reveal himself in a last attempt to bring Mosca down. In the end, Volpone, Mosca, and all three would-be heirs—Voltore, Corbaccio, and Corvino—face punishment.

Emily Windsnap is a girl who lives on the boat The King of the Sea with her mother Mary Penelope. She requests swimming lessons repeatedly until her mother, who is afraid of the water, allows it. After a few shocking incidents, Emily discovers she is half mermaid, half human. Her legs become a tail when she is immersed in water and become legs again when she leaves it. She meets another mermaid whose name is Shona, and they quickly become best friends. Together they discover that Emily's father is currently in the mer prison for marrying a human and that Mary is under a spell which makes her forget everything. The girls plan to save Emily's father, but do not know how. Later, Emily finds a chance to carry out her "daydream" plan and manages to drive their houseboat near the prison. Her mother follows and regains her memories of Jake Windsnap, her husband (Emily's father). They are caught by Neptune and brought to trial, where Emily manages to convince Neptune for the sake of their family's mutual love to let them go. Neptune releases the entire Windsnap family on one condition: they must live on a deserted island!

"The book opens and closes with a picture of little Sal and her mother in the kitchen, the mother is canning blueberries... One sees in this opening picture Sal entertaining herself by placing the canning rings on her wrist and a spoon, a simple childlike act which helps to set the stage for Sal's obvious child actions throughout the books. This is not to be the overly diligent or angelic girl of so many other books, Sal is a real child figure. She gets into mischief and causes her mom no end of trouble.” Little Sal's Mother takes her to Blueberry Hill to pick berries. Sal drops three berries in her bucket, then eats them. This continues as she and her mother concentrate on the berries and gradually get separated on the hill. What they don't realize is that a mother bear and her cub have also come to Blueberry Hill to eat berries for the winter. The book uses a number of visual and verbal techniques to compare and contrast the bear and the human families. Both families pictures are similar in compositions, but they head in opposite directions when they reach the blueberry patch. Little Sal’s Mother tells her that they can’t eat all the berries because they need to save them to can for the winter, but the bear mother tells her child to eat as much as it can to store up fat for winter. The bear's way of preparing for winter is more natural for Sal who soon wanders off to eat. Sal and the bear cub get mixed up and follow after the wrong mother. It takes the mothers several minutes to realize they're being followed by the wrong child; it isn't until the bear cub tries to eat from Sal's mother's bucket and the mother bear hears the "ku-plink, ku-plank, ku-plunk" sound of Sal dropping blueberries into her tin pail that they realize what happened. Ultimately each child is reunited with its proper mother and they both leave the hill. Just before leaving Sal drops a blueberry into her empty pail. The end papers show Sal again playing in the kitchen while her mother cans berries.

The plot partially revolves around the missing master copy of a film cartridge, titled Infinite Jest and referred to in the novel as "the Entertainment" or "the samizdat". The film is so entertaining to its viewers that they become lifeless, losing all interest in anything other than viewing the film. The video cartridge was the final work of film by James O. Incandenza before his microwave suicide, completed during a stint of sobriety that was requested by the lead actress, Joelle. Quebec separatists are interested in acquiring a master, redistributable copy of the work to aid in acts of terrorism against the United States. The United States Office of Unspecified Services (USOUS) is seeking to intercept the master copy of the film in order to prevent mass dissemination and the destabilization of the Organization of North American Nations. Joelle and later Hal seek treatment for substance abuse problems at The Ennet House Drug and Alcohol Recovery House, and Marathe visits the rehabilitation center to pursue a lead on the master copy of the Entertainment, tying the characters and plots together.

Poliphilo’s night is disturbed from the start when his beloved Polia, whose name means “Many Things,” spurns him. A restless sleep carries him into an untamed forest, where he loses his way, confronts dragons and wolves, meets maidens, and encounters a dazzling array of architectural marvels; he escapes and drifts back into sleep. He then enters a second dream, nested within the first. In this dream, a group of nymphs escorts him to their queen, and there he must profess his love for Polia, which he does. Two nymphs guide him to three gates, from which he selects the third, thereby rediscovering Polia. The couple is then led by more nymphs to a temple for an engagement. On the way, they witness five triumphal processions celebrating their union. A barge carries them to the island of Cythera, Cupid serving as boatswain, and another procession extols their bond. The narrative pauses as a second voice intrudes, presenting Polia’s erotomachia from her own perspective. Poliphilo resumes the tale after about one-fifth of the book. Polia rejects him, but a vision of Cupid confronts her and compels her to return, kissing Poliphilo, who lies in a deathlike swoon at her feet, back to life. Venus blesses their love, and the lovers finally unite. Just as Poliphilo is about to clasp Polia, she vanishes into thin air, and Poliphilo awakens. * Poliphilus * Polia

Set in Swinging London, the story follows a single day in the life of Adam Appleby, who lives under the constant fear that his wife might be pregnant again, bringing a fourth child. Bound by Catholic doctrine, they cannot use contraception and end up playing a form of “Vatican roulette.” Adam and Barbara are parents to Clare, Dominic, and Edward, and their friends tease whether they plan to work their way through the alphabet next. Throughout one busy day, Adam encounters several opportunities to earn money. He is offered a chance to edit the unpublished manuscripts of a deceased scholar, yet, upon inspecting them, he recoils, realizing the writings amount to worthless drivel. At the Bayswater house where the papers should be retrieved, Adam encounters a motley crew of characters—from butchers to a young, open-to-seduction virgin. Lodge’s novel frequently employs pastiche, deliberately mimicking the motifs and stylistic signatures of various writers. For example, a Kafkaesque episode unfolds as Adam renews his reading-room ticket. The closing chapter features a monologue by Adam’s wife, crafted in the manner of Molly Bloom’s soliloquy from Ulysses. This stylistic collage mirrors James Joyce’s Ulysses, itself a tale centered on a single day. Upon its release, many critics, lacking appreciation for the literary allusions, faulted Lodge for producing a heterogeneous, uneven work.

The narrative traces the narrator’s childhood by weaving together a series of formative moments: dawn beach fishing, observations of his grandparents—especially one grandfather who descends into madness—a hunchbacked great-uncle, and the tensions between children and adults marked by betrayal, fear of the unknown, and the shadow of violence that can culminate in murder. Overlaying this personal tale is a traditional thread drawn from the Mr. Punch show, framed by the line “the oldest, the wisest play.” The narrator first meets Mr. Punch while fishing with his grandfather, yet he later encounters the Punch and Judy figure—and a mysterious “professor” associated with the puppet show—during other activities. The Mr. Punch legend unfolds with graphic violence: he kills his infant son, then his wife Judy, and ultimately the officer who comes to arrest him. In the course of the tale, Punch tricks a ghost, outsmarts a crocodile and a doctor, persuades the executioner to be hanged in his stead, and even appears to vanquish the devil by the end of the performance. As in many of Neil Gaiman’s works, memory itself plays a central role here, underscoring the fragility and unreliability of recollection.

Jack Cull, a name that plays on jackal, finds himself in a surreal setting dubbed “Hell.” This Hell is a vast, sun-centered sphere where the dead and demons coexist; the humans retain their pre-death minds and bodies, free from disease or hunger, and deaths occur in reverse hours. The ground trembles with frequent earthquakes, and humanity has seized control of this realm. In place of Dante’s iconic Italian exhortation, they inscribe a new warning: “Do not abandon hope,” written in Hebrew. At his job, Cull learns that a mysterious figure known as “X”—an analogue to Jesus Christ—has been slain by a rowdy mob. Accompanied by Phyllis and Fyodor (a nod to Fyodor Dostoevsky), Jack begins an investigation into the murder. Their journey leads them through a sewer where they uncover a startling truth: Hell is actually a gigantic spacecraft, steered by ultra-moral, immensely powerful aliens. These beings can seize vast numbers of souls and merge them into immortal bodies, provided the souls are fed regularly. The capture process, however, is imperfect, and many souls are lost to an emptiness beyond reach. Even when the bodies are nearly immortal, the aliens eventually destroy them if they deem the souls to have progressed sufficiently. Yet destruction isn’t universal; some bodies survive and continue to travel aboard the ship as it roams the galaxy.

Everything on a Waffle, set in a small Canadian fishing village, tells the story of an eleven-year-old girl named Primrose Squarp. Primrose's parents disappear in a typhoon, but Primrose refuses to believe they are dead and doesn't attend their memorial service. While she defends her family's survival,her custody situation moves around from aging neighbor Miss Perfidy to her preoccupied Uncle Jack. The only thing that remains constant is her enjoyment of a restaurant called the Girl on the Red Swing, where each menu item is served on a waffle. Restaurant owner Kate Bowzer takes Primrose under her wing. She teaches her how to cook (recipes are all cited in a notepad) She doesn't question or criticize her, even through her odd predicaments, such as accidentally setting the class guinea pig on fire Primrose is taken from the custody of her uncle 'Uncle Jack' to an older couple. While she likes them, she is involved in a variety of accidents, including losing a toe. Through her oddities and accidents, Primrose becomes a town curiosity, with neighbors questioning her emotional state. But even through all of this, Primrose never gives up hope in finding her parents and being a normal family again.Later on, her parents come back, which is a real shock to everyone in town.

Framed as an extended message to her daughter in America, the novel traces the inward odyssey of Mrs. Curren, an aging professor of classics. Residing in Cape Town during the height of Apartheid, she battles terminal cancer while having spent a lifetime opposing the regime in principle but never before taking a public stand. In her final days, she confronts the regime’s brutal reality—witnessing the torching of a black township, the death of her servant’s son, and the security forces’ shooting of a young black activist she harbors in her home. Against a backdrop of violence from both white and Black factions, she reflects on her past and on the daughter who left South Africa because of the turmoil. As the narrative unfolds, she forms a new, rather unconventional bond with Vercueil, an elderly homeless man who sleeps in her driveway, and she grows to truly recognize Florence, her black live-in servant. Coetzee interweaves central themes—aging, the confessor-as-hero, modes of narration, the meaning of freedom, and the stance of the white liberal in apartheid-era South Africa.

In the northern realms reside Jenny Waynest, a witch, and her companion, the nobleman John Aversin. Their attention is drawn by Gareth, a young southern aristocrat who pleads for their help: slay a dragon in the capital city of Bel, far to the south. They consent, but only if the king will dispatch troops to the north to repel marauding bandits. Upon their arrival, Gareth’s identity is disclosed—he is not merely a noble, but the realm’s prince, seeking aid against his father’s will. The dragon turns out to be Morkeleb the Black, ancient and formidable, dwelling in the caverns of the gnomes. Complicating matters, the sorceress Zyerne has seized the king’s will, wielding power over him to seize the magic of the Stone housed within the gnomish Deep. John is coaxed into killing Morkeleb, with Jenny backing him, yet John is wounded and Jenny must step in to save the dragon’s life, trading Morkeleb’s survival for John’s. In preserving the dragon, Jenny’s limited abilities are greatly amplified, enabling her to confront Zyerne but also tempting her to shed humanity and become a dragon herself. Zyerne infiltrates the Deep to claim its magic, yet she is defeated when John, Jenny, and Morkeleb destroy the Stone. Jenny agrees to the dragon’s offer of transformation, but ultimately returns north, unable to endure life apart from her humanity.

Remy, an eighteen-year-old about to start college, has grown up with a father who died before her birth; he left behind a short song, affectionately known as “This Lullaby,” now wildly popular. Her mother is about to wed for the fifth time, this time to a car salesman, a circumstance that convinces Remy that love is a myth. In her past, she’s hopped from one relationship to another without genuine care, and those romances never endure. A chance encounter introduces Dexter, who says he felt an instant connection the moment he laid eyes on her. Dexter is messy and a musician—traits Remy dislikes—but his persistence wears her down. Gradually she discovers herself drawn to him. Although she resists, she cannot bring herself to let him go. They eventually begin dating, and she is taken aback by how open, honest, and compassionate he proves to be. Their romance falters when Dexter overhears Remy confessing that he’s only a summer fling for her, prompting a breakup. Remy moves on with another man, yet Dexter lingers in her thoughts. Meanwhile, her brother becomes engaged, her mother’s new husband shows signs of infidelity, and their friends grapple with their own troubles. In the end, Remy comes to understand that her love for Dexter is real, and the couple reconcile.

Set in Michigan’s north during the mid-1920s, The Torrents of Spring follows two men who work at a pump factory: Yogi Johnson, a World War I veteran, and Scripps O’Neill, a novelist. The narrative begins with O’Neill’s homecoming to find his wife and young daughter gone. He befriends a British diner worker, Diana, and quickly proposes marriage, only to grow disenchanted with her. Diana attempts to woo her husband by poring over books drawn from The New York Times Book Review lists, but he soon departs for another waitress named Mandy, who captivates him with literary tales—some perhaps fabricated. Johnson sinks into depression after a Parisian prostitute abandons him for a British officer, and he cycles through a phase of not craving any woman even as spring nears. In the end, a Native American woman—entering a restaurant wearing only moccasins, and who is the wife of one of the two Indians he has befriended toward the conclusion—awakens his love.

For Kathleen, Sari, and Lucy, the weekly knitting circle feels like the only thing holding them together amid growing fragility. Their delicate scarves may be stylish, yet their lives are beginning to come undone. Kathleen, the perennial beauty who has long depended on her famous actress sisters, contemplates independence after moving out. She longs for the luxury she once had and starts wondering if marrying into wealth could restore it. Meanwhile, Lucy dates the man she adores—handsome, brilliant, and on the ascent—but when an animal-rights campaign targets him, she questions which side she genuinely supports. Sari encounters again the high school’s charming “it” guy—now still stunning, tender, and kind, and a father who needs her help. Yet she wonders if she can ever forgive him for the harm he caused her brother a decade earlier. Between careers, romance, and the quest to master the perfect cast-on, the three friends discover that there are rarely easy solutions. Perhaps the only certainty is this: when life gets tough, knitting becomes their resolve.

On the surface the plot follows the story of a penniless, starving author called Geoffrey Tempest. So poor that he is behind on his rent and can barely afford light in his room, he receives three letters. The first is from a friend in Australia who has made his fortune and offers to introduce him to a good friend who might be able to lift him from poverty. The second is a note from a solicitor detailing that he has inherited a fortune from a deceased relative, the third is a letter of introduction from a foreign aristocrat called Lucio, who befriends him and proceeds to be his guide in how to best use his new found wealth. Tempest remains blissfully unaware throughout the novel, despite warnings from people he meets, that Lucio is the Earthly incarnation of the Devil. Over the course of the book, his wealth leads to misery. Eventually, when confronted with the true nature of his companion, he renounces evil and returns to society penniless but content with the chance to purify his soul. Although the plot follows Tempest's fall from grace and redemption, he is in many regards a secondary character to Lucio. Both the title of the work and much of its philosophical content relate to the supreme yearning within Satan to achieve salvation. The book's main contribution to Faustian literature is the introduction of the concept that above all other people it is Satan who most truly believes in the Gospel — and yet he is forbidden to ever partake of it.

An aging poet, Steponas Daumantas, treads Vilnius’s streets, snapping photographs of young mothers and their infants. His fixation fixates on Jolanta, a particular woman, and a friendship blossoms between them. She entrusts him with a manuscript her husband has authored; Daumantas vows to read it and perhaps present it to a publisher, only to lose the manuscript when drunkenness overtakes him. As their bond with Jolanta deepens, the memories long restrained within him begin to surge to the surface. In a different thread, Svetlana—an ethnic Russian living in poverty in Vilnius’s Old Town back lanes—does laundry for Daumantas and, after a night when he is drunk, she salvages a manuscript he abandons. She struggles to earn money to send her son to England for work, all while coping with a brutal husband, Ivan. A friendship forms between Svetlana and Ruta, a young prostitute, and memories of her own past she would rather forget surface. Daumantas, meanwhile, grows up in a small village near Wilno, nurturing early poetic ambitions and falling in love with a local Jewish girl, Rachael. When she rejects him, he leaves for university in Wilno. Years later, he encounters Rachael again in Wilno, now married to a Jewish man. In 1939, the Soviet invasion returns Wilno to Lithuanian control, and streets become roamed by Lithuanian thugs; yet the worst is still to come with the German invasion. As the Jewish community in the Vilna ghetto is gradually suffocated, Rachael makes a stark request of Daumantas: take her child and save it.

During World War II, in a prison within Occupied France, a brutal rule is issued: one in ten inmates must be executed, selected by drawing lots. Among those chosen is a wealthy lawyer. Desperate to spare himself, he offers his entire fortune to any volunteer who will take his place. A single man steps forward. After his release, the lawyer must confront the fallout of this bargain. The tale unfolds in four parts. In Part I, the incarcerated setting remains as German guards impose the decimation on thirty prisoners, with Chavel—the rich lawyer—among the three selected by lot. Overcome by panic, he pleads for someone to die in his stead and, in a twist, a young man named Janvier agrees and is executed. Part II leaps forward to the war’s end: Chavel survives and regains freedom but has been left nearly penniless. He returns to the house he once sold for his life, only to discover it now occupied by Janvier’s mother and sister, Thérèse. Under the assumed alias Charlot, he becomes their servant. In Part III, an impostor named Carosse appears, claiming to be Chavel. Carosse tries to expose Charlot, ingratiate himself with Thérèse, and lay claim to the property. The final Part IV follows Charlot as he, having fallen for Thérèse, seeks to rescue her from Carosse, using this act as atonement for his prior cowardice.

A young woman narrates in the first person her struggle with severe illness, including depression and thoughts of suicide. When her doctor cannot help, she is sent on a holiday that leads her to a mystical figure: Raffello Cellini, a renowned Italian artist. Cellini presents her with an odd potion that sends her into an immediate, tranquil sleep, during which she experiences heavenly visions. Upon waking, she longs for more. Later, she encounters her guardian angel, Heliobas, the story’s central figure, who carries her across countless solar systems at speeds surpassing a shooting star, while human souls drift past like delicate silk. He reveals the truths of religion and the hidden purpose of humanity, yet her desire persists. She comes to recognize God as radiant light and boundless love, but merely hearing and seeing these truths from an angel’s touch does not satisfy her. She yearns to wield this power independently and seeks unity with God through a sequence of meditative practices, while secluded in a monastery.

Winter settles over Dalton, a New England town just outside Boston, as Leonidas Witherall—famed as “the man who looks like Shakespeare”—returns to a house he has never seen before. He has inherited money, circled the globe, and left directions for building his home during his travels, yet now he must come back to furnish the next adventure of Lieutenant Haseltine. On the train, he encounters a timid woman called Miss Chard, known to all as Swiss Chard, and also a striking young woman carrying a brown paper parcel and guarding a secret. His new residence proves to be a source of delight, boasting a kitchen equipped with red appliances, a library that begs for ladders, and a garage that hides the misanthropic Medora’s pickaxed corpse from the neighboring scene. To manage his affairs, Leonidas gathers a team: a scatterbrained housewife named Cassie Price and Cuff, a reformed ex-thief who now serves on the police force. With these helpers, he protects the red refrigerator, recovers the missing envelope of money, and ultimately brings the killer to justice.

Bella Swan leaves sunny Phoenix for Forks, Washington, moving in with her father, Charlie, while her mother Renée travels with her new husband, minor-league baseball player Phil Dwyer. At her new school, Bella quickly draws attention and makes several friends, though a string of bullies and admirers complicates her experience. On the first day, Edward Cullen publicly recoils from her before vanishing for several days; when he returns, a tentative bond forms that culminates in a near-tragedy: a classmate’s van threatens Bella in the parking lot, and Edward materializes beside her to halt the vehicle with his bare hands. Intrigued by how he saved her, Bella presses him with questions. A local legend shared by a family friend, Jacob Black, leads Bella to conclude that Edward and his kin are vampires who drink animal blood rather than human blood. Edward admits he initially steered clear of Bella because her scent overwhelmed him. As time passes, their love deepens. The arrival of a nomadic vampire coven unsettles Forks, introducing James, a relentless hunter drawn to the Cullens’ unusual relationship with a human. To divert James, the Cullens separate Bella from Edward and arrange for her to hide at a Phoenix hotel. There, James phones with a chilling ruse—he claims to have Bella’s mother captive. When Bella agrees to surrender, James attacks; Edward and the rest of the family intervene, ultimately killing James after he bites Bella’s hand. Edward retrieves the venom from her bloodstream, preventing her transformation, and Bella is rushed to a hospital. Back in Forks, the couple attends prom, where Bella voices her wish to become a vampire, but Edward refuses.

Benedykt Gierosławski, a Polish mathematician and infamous gambler, serves as the novel’s central figure. He is enlisted by Alfred Tarski to collaborate on work concerning many-valued logics. Officials from the Ministry of Winter compel him to undertake a Transsiberian expedition in search of his missing father, who supposedly has the ability to communicate with Lute. Throughout the journey, Gierosławski uncovers himself as a pawn in a political power play shaped by a rivalry between two palace factions: the conservatives and Siberian capitalists backing the notion of a “frozen Russia,” versus the more radical “thaw” faction, which seeks open political and literal thawing and is supported by the Tsar. In disguise, Nikola Tesla appears, revealing a technology capable of controlling and ultimately annihilating the Ice; he has been hired by the Tsar to free Russia from Winter. As the voyage continues and upon reaching Irkutsk, Gierosławski learns that multiple political actors—Followers of St. Marcyn (a sect venerating the Ice led by Rasputin), adherents of Nikolai Fyodorovich Fyodorov (pursuing human immortality), and Siberian industrial magnates—are keenly interested in him. Adding to the intrigue, Józef Piłsudski, leading a faction of Sybiraks and Siberian separatists in this reality, may hold crucial information about his father.

John Wright, a middle-class small businessman, hatches a plan to murder the President of the United States. He spends his life savings to illicitly obtain a U.S. Army shipment containing two precursor chemicals that, when mixed, form a deadly nerve agent codenamed VZ. The intention is to trigger a detonation of VZ in downtown San Diego to coincide with the President’s visit for a Republican party conference. The nerve gas is lethal within two to three minutes of inhalation or contact and has no antidote. Encasing the gas are two Alacran plastic tanks, each wrapped in plastic explosives, so that the containers would explode after the gas release, leaving no clear trail to the crime. The plot is foiled by John Graves, a State Department agent who has been shadowing Wright, uncovering the scheme and stopping it two minutes before the timer would reach zero.

Beth, a thriving pop singer and a devout Protestant from Texas, travels with her boyfriend Steve as part of a missionary group called the Cowboys for Christ, which crosses into so-called heathen regions to spread Christianity. Hoping to convert souls in Glasgow, Scotland, they are met with a bitter reception, and Beth is even attacked by a large dog. After performing at a local cathedral, they are met by Lord Lachlan and his wife Delia, aristocrats from the nearby Scottish village of Tressock. The couple invites them to return with them to Tressock to continue preaching. Meanwhile, detective Orlando goes to Tressock undercover as the village’s police officer to quietly probe rumors of a pagan cult. Beth and Steve decide to begin their outreach during the village’s May Day festivities. Orlando soon learns that the townsfolk honor the ancient Celt goddess Sulis. To ingratiate themselves with the locals, Beth and Steve agree to assume the roles of the May Queen and the Laddie for the celebration. The duties require them to split up for the day, and during this separation the Laddie is slaughtered by the villagers on an island in the middle of the river Sulis. Beth finds him and attempts to flee, but she is eventually captured and embalmed.

Wedge Antilles persists in defending Borleias from the Yuuzhan Vong, continuing the arc begun in Rebel Dream. After tracking down and eliminating a spy within the Vong-ruled Tam Elgrin, he sets about building a superlaser—identical to the Death Star in design, but it is defective by intent. Antilles engineers a ruse: using both the feverish fixation of Commander Czulkang Lah on capturing Jaina Solo and the laser’s dubious functionality, he lures Lah’s fleet away from the Lusankya, Lah’s flagship. While the Yuuzhan Vong force is diverted, the Super Star Destroyer Lusankya is equipped with a spear and steered straight into the worldship, bringing it down and sealing Lah’s fate. On Coruscant, Luke Skywalker, Mara Jade Skywalker, Tahiri Veila, and Wraith Squadron press on with their reconnaissance, encountering a Dark Jedi who resembles the mythic Nyax but is, in truth, the engineered Dark Jedi Irek Ismaren. Though Nyax proves to be stronger than Luke, the combined Jedi-Yuuzhan Vong effort overpowers him and defeats Nyax. Simultaneously, Viqi Shesh’s plan to flee Coruscant is thwarted by Wraith Squadron, driving her to suicide. In parallel, Han and Leia Organa Solo, accompanied by C-3PO and R2-D2, undertake missions to unseat any planetary government willing to bend to Yuuzhan Vong rule. Their perilous assignment on Aphran IV tests their nerve, but they emerge victorious with the mission accomplished.

The novel has two narratives in alternate chapters. The first follows two citizens of the Amalgam, a Milky Way-spanning civilisation, investigating the origin of DNA found on a meteor by the Aloof. The Aloof control the galactic core and until the novel begins, have rejected all attempts at contact by the Amalgam. The second narrative is set on a small world known as the Splinter, and covers the attempts by its inhabitants to understand the environment within which their home exists. As the story progresses, it becomes clear that the Splinter orbits a collapsed star within its accretion disk and is subject to various dangers. The two stories come together in a complex twist which involves a kind of past/future first contact role reversal. Much of the narrative explores the effects of orbital dynamics around a high mass object and requires an understanding of Newtonian gravitation and at least a basic familiarity with general relativity and its application to black holes and neutron stars to be compelling. Understanding the story's wider frame of reference and the Splinter's encounter with the Wanderer are tied in with this. The Amalgam is explored in two other short stories, "Glory" and "Riding the Crocodile".

Kin-Fo is a very wealthy man, who certainly does not lack material possessions. However, he is terribly bored and when news reaches him about his major investment abroad, a bank in the United States, going bankrupt, Kin-Fo decides to die. He signs up for a $200,000 life insurance covering all kinds of accidents, death in war, and even suicide. He rejects seppuku and hanging as means of dying, and is about to take opium laced with poison when he decides that he doesn't want to die without having ever felt a thrill in his life. Kin-Fo hires his old mentor, the philosopher Wang, to murder him before the life insurance expires. After a while news reaches Kin-Fo that the American bank he had invested in was not bankrupt, but instead had pulled off a stock market trick and is now wealthier than ever. Unfortunately, Wang has already disappeared. Together with two body guards assigned by the insurance company, and his loyal but lazy and incompetent servant Soun, Kin-Fo travels around the country in an effort to run away from Wang and the humiliation from the affair. One day he receives a message from Wang, stating that he can't stand the pain of having to kill one of his friends, and instead decided to take his own life while giving the task of killing Kin-Fo to a bandit he once knew. Kin-Fo, Soun and the two bodyguards now try to get to the bandit, planning to offer money in return for his life. The ship they travel with is hijacked, and they are forced to use their life vests with built-in sails to return to land. After being kidnapped by the bandit they were looking for, they are blindfolded and returned to Kin-Fo's home, where his old friends (including Wang, who we now find out staged this entire history to teach him a lesson about how valuable life is) are waiting for him. He marries a young, beautiful woman and they live happily forever after.

Second Glance follows several characters throughout the book, in Jodi Picoult's typical fashion, flashing back and forth many decades to piece together the story. It is set in Comtosook, VT. The main plot is that an Abenaki land space is planned to be turned into a shopping mall. However, if the Abenaki can prove that an ancestor was buried on the land, it cannot be built on. Ross Wakeman comes to town to stay with his sister. He is the survivor of many varied suicide attempts, which began after his fiancee Aimee was killed in a car accident years ago. He became a ghost hunter hoping to someday encounter her spirit. Comtosook begins to experience many strange phenomena as the result of the threat of development on the sacred land, including water that refuses to boil. With the help of a local detective, Ross uncovers a decades-old murder mystery that helps to prove that the land in question truly is a Native American-burial ground, and in turn is able to save the land from development. But the Native American that was buried there surprises everyone and makes Ross think with parts of his brain that he has not paid attention to in years.

It is the surreal story of two boys, Hashi and Kiku, who were both abandoned by their mothers during infancy and locked in coin lockers at a Tokyo train station in the summer of 1972. Both boys become wards of the Cherryfield Orphanage in Yokohama, where the tough and athletic Kiku comes to the defense of the slight, and often picked on, Hashi. They are adopted by foster parents, the Kuwayamas (the wife is Zainichi Korean) who live on an island off Kyushu. At the age of 16 both find themselves in a diseased urban wasteland in Tokyo named Toxitown. Hashi, whose voice has deep effects on those who hear it, becomes a bisexual rock star, employed by an eccentric producer named D. Kiku becomes a pole vaulter and with his girlfriend Anemone, a model who has converted her condo into a swamp for her crocodile, searches for a substance named DATURA in order to take his revenge upon the city of Tokyo and destroy it. Along the way, however, in a search for Hashi's real mother, Hashi and D come upon a woman who turns out to be Kiku's... with grave consequences for them all.

Near to the Wild Heart defies a conventional storyline, instead collectionizing brief glimpses from Joana’s life that oscillate between her current adulthood and childhood. As with many of Lispector’s works, the emphasis rests on internal, emotional landscapes. The narrative opens with Joana as a girl at play in the garden, composing poems for her father. Her unruly spirit, almost palpable violence, and inventive use of language stand out as defining traits. Throughout the tale she is likened to various animals—described as a bird, a snake, a wildcat, a horse, and a dog. Her actions border on transgression: as a child she hurls a book at an elderly man’s head; later, as a grown woman, she abandons her husband Otávio and reacts with flat apathy to news of his affair—his liaison with another woman, his old acquaintance Lídia, whom he has made pregnant. Rather than a straightforward moral judgment, Joana appears amoral rather than immoral, encapsulated in the line, “Evil is not living, and that’s it. Dying is already something else. Dying is different from good and evil.” The text also quotes lengthy passages from Spinoza—arguably the most substantial direct excerpts in Lispector’s entire body of fiction—suggesting a deep kinship with the Dutch thinker’s amoral worldview.

In town, Willy and his dog Searchlight discover his grandfather is bedridden and despondent about living. The sole physician, Doc Smith, informs Willy that his grandfather wishes to die. Later, tax collector Clifford Snyder infiltrates Willy’s home, pistol in hand, pressing for the grandpa’s debt to the state and, after glancing at papers, declares a Wyoming tab of 500 dollars. The following day, Willy enters a dog-sled race carrying a prize of 500 dollars. He notices a sled drawn by five fast Samoyeds; the entrant turns out to be Stone Fox—the enigmatic Native American who speaks to whites rarely and has never lost a race. As the competition unfolds, Willy’s lightweight, single-dog sled proves unusually adept at navigating sharp bends and even enables a dangerous shortcut across a frozen lake. Tragically, Searchlight collapses from exhaustion just ten feet from the finish line, her heart bursting on impact. Stone Fox marks the path with a booted line, draws a rifle, and warns that any other racer who crosses first will be shot. Yet in a stunning turn, he relinquishes the victory to Willy, allowing Searchlight to be carried over the finish line to the astonishment of everyone watching.

The story itself is loosely based around Billy, a young boy who has always dreamed of owning a sweet shop, especially since there is an abandoned one named The Grubber (an old [[English word for sweet shop) near where he lives. One day, he finds that the old building has been renovated and has become the head office for the Ladderless Window-Cleaning Company. Billy then meets its workers, a Giraffe with an extendable neck, a Pelican (or "Pelly" as he is called by the others) who can retract his upper beak, and a Monkey, whom he then befriends. They all band together when they receive a letter from the Duke of Hampshire asking them to clean the windows of Hampshire House. When they get there, things go smoothly until the Giraffe and the Monkey, while cleaning the windows of the Duchess's bedroom, spot a burglar who attempts to steal the Duchess's diamond jewellery. The Pelican then flies in and catches the burglar in his beak, holding him there while the others panic. Eventually, the police arrive to arrest the burglar, whom the Chief of Police identifies as "The Cobra", one of the world's most dangerous cat burglars. As a reward for retrieving the Duchess's diamonds, the Duke invites the L.W.C.C. to live on his estate as his personal helper. Billy's dreams come true because the Giraffe, Pelican and Monkey will no longer be needing the Grubber building; with a little help from the Duke, the Grubber is reopened into the most fantastic sweet shop in the whole town (even selling sweets from the Willy Wonka company). And they live happily ever after.

Maerth argued that consuming brain produced an aphrodisiac effect—likely due to the large hormone content—and that this initially led apes to crave it, prompting brain-hunt episodes where males from rival bands were killed and females subjected to rape in a frenzy linked to brain-induced sexuality and violence. The diet, however, inadvertently increased brain size and intelligence while causing hair loss and a decline in our innate psychic abilities. Over time, humans emerged, remaining cannibalistic until about 50,000 years ago. Modern humans, now estranged from their surroundings after losing telepathic contact with nature and with other animals, suffer from distorted sexuality caused by hormonal imbalances and are driven toward madness by the constant pressure of oversized brains pressing inside the skull. Maerth (1974), p. 53, predicts that humanity is inevitably destroying itself through pollution, overpopulation, racial mixing, and eventually nuclear war. He also forecasts a near-future return to cannibalism (Maerth, p. 199) and urges readers to withdraw from society, adopt a vegetarian diet, study Eastern wisdom, and perhaps use wooden frames and wire devices to alter the skull’s shape as some ancient cultures did, thereby relieving brain pressure and partially restoring psychic powers.

In Adventure in Australia, the Count of Champignac, joined by a young professor, Walker Donahue, believes he has made an extraordinary find: a colossal indigenous monolith near a mining village in Australia. He invites Spirou and Fantasio to come along, and they travel there with Seccotine, whose presence proves indispensable. Upon their arrival, Donahue reveals that the Count was killed by some miners. Following their investigation, they learn that the Count is not dead; instead, they encounter him severely battered, confronting Sam—a gangster who makes his fortune by extorting prospectors. Sam ultimately dies when a truck explodes due to a nitroglycerin bottle. Benefiting from the aid of the local aboriginals, Spirou, Donahue, and the Count drive Sam’s henchmen from the field, those who had been targeting Fantasio and Seccotine. In the end, the monolith is unearthed, and an agreement is reached whereby the indigenous community shares resources with the prospectors, who are grateful to them for removing Sam from the equation.
