Dee has a fiery temper and often argues with Travis, the wealthy farm owner; many of their arguments lead to passionate embraces. Travis later rescues Dee from an attempted rape. When Paddy suffers a heart attack, he becomes very concerned about his mortality and Dee's future. He becomes overwrought and insists that Travis take care of Dee. After privately agreeing to a temporary marriage of convenience, Travis and Dee exchange vows in Paddy's hospital room. As the story progresses, the protagonists become increasingly unhappy, with neither willing to admit their love for the other. Although still unwilling to vocalize their feelings, Dee and Travis appear more confident in their relationship after they finally consummate their marriage. Soon, however, Dee's insecurities are exploited by Travis's sophisticated former girlfriend, Margot, who has returned to the area to win him back. Dee runs away. Travis follows, and the two confess their love and resolve to make their marriage work.

Princess Taramis of Shadizar promises to bring Conan's lost love Valeria back to life if the Cimmerian will procure two magical items that she hopes will gain her ultimate power, a wizard's gem and a horn that can awaken the dreaming god Dagoth. He undertakes the quest together with his thief partner Malak and Taramis' niece Jehnna and henchman Bombaata. On their journey they are joined by two additional allies whom Conan saves from dire fates; the magician Akiro and the female warrior Zula. At their goal, the castle of the wizard Amon-Rama, Jehnna is kidnapped. Thanks to Akiro's magic she is located in Amon-Rama's lair and a way in is discovered. Inside, Conan is separated from the others and forced to battle a Man-Ape in a hall of mirrors, which he is only able to defeat by destroying the mirrors. He also mortally wounds the wizard, who is hiding behind one of them. Jehnna, who is the only person who can safely handle the wizard's gem, retrieves the first magical item. Afterwards the group beats off an attack by Corinthian soldiers, and continues on to the fortress that holds the horn. It is retrieved at the cost of a battle with its Dagoth-worshipping keepers, whose leader Akiro defeats in a sorcerous duel. Bombaata and Jehnna escape through a tunnel, which the former closes to the others by starting a landslide. Back at Taramis' palace, the queen conducts a ritual to awaken Dagoth that entails the placing of the horn on the forehead of the sleeping deity, and ultimately the sacrifice of Jehnna. Conan, Akiro and Zula, having survived the landslide, interrupt the proceedings. Conan fights and defeats Bombaata while Zula rescues Jehnna. In the absence of the sacrifice, Dagoth is an uncontrollable monster on his revival, eating Taramis and threatening the destruction of everything else. On the advice of Akiro, Conan rips the horn from Dagoth's forehead, and the creature finally falls. In the aftermath, Jehnna succeeds to the throne of Shadazar and takes Zula, Akiro, and Malak as advisors. She offers Conan her hand and a place at her side as king, but the Cimmerian prefers to win his own kingdom.

During the Second Sudanese Civil War, Achak is torn from his family when murahaleen—Arabic for “traveller”—the Arab militia, attack his Dinka village, Marial Bai. In the assault, he loses track of his father and his childhood friends, Moses and William K. Though William K. escapes, Moses is presumed dead. Seeking safety, Achak and his mother take refuge at his aunt’s house, a woman repeatedly described in the book as wearing a yellow dress. Before they can be hidden, they hear the aunt scream, and Achak’s mother goes to investigate; after that moment, she vanishes from his sight forever. To stay hidden, he hides inside a grain bag and later credits divine aid for keeping him silent. Along with a band of other youths known as the “Lost Boys,” he ventures on foot, trudging through extreme peril and hardship toward a refugee camp in Ethiopia. The dream of safety he carries with him is crushed by the camp’s brutal conditions, forcing a subsequent withdrawal to another camp in Kakuma after Mengistu’s fall and soldiers’ gunfire. From there they cross into Kenya, and years later Achak finally relocates to the United States. The narrative unfolds in tandem with the new rounds of hardship he faces in America.

Rapp appears on the scene during a covert operation in Iran, where he uncovers intelligence about an impending terrorist attack aimed at the nation’s capital. Across the Atlantic, Washington, D.C. buzzes with the first day of NBC White House correspondent Anna Reilly. The same day, the terrorists breach the White House through a secret entry, seizing control and taking hostages. In the chaos, the president narrowly escapes a collapse into an unfinished bomb shelter, leaving him effectively trapped. Seizing the moment, the acting commander in chief, the vice president, seeks to polish his political image by yielding to the attackers’ demands, while Rapp conceals his own plan to combat the threat from inside the White House walls. Inside the mansion, Rapp rescues Anna Reilly from a brutal assault, birthing the partnership that will unfold in subsequent novels. As events unfold, a contingent of Navy SEALs infiltrates the White House, neutralizes the terrorists, frees the hostages, and rescues the president. Although the terrorist leader eludes capture by detonating carefully placed explosives, he ultimately flees to South America, where Rapp later locates and kills him.

Opening with a prologue set at the 2009 FIRST Championship in Atlanta, the narrative captures the electrifying atmosphere there. It then moves backward to the January 2009 kickoff, detailing Dean Kamen’s founding of FIRST. The focus then shifts to the history of team 1717 and the Dos Pueblos Engineering Academy, the program they belong to. The account continues by tracing the 2009 team through a six-week build season, highlighting challenges ranging from mechanical failures to a spell of illness. A dedicated chapter spotlights team 217, the ThunderChickens, who strive for robot construction with military-grade precision, and team 395, 2TrainRobotics, whose students confront issues stemming from their position in a poor inner-city environment, as well as team 67, Heroes of Tomorrow. After the build, 1717 competes at two regional events, Los Angeles and Sacramento; they fall in the finals in Los Angeles but go undefeated in Sacramento, culminating in a victory there. The season concludes with 1717 at the FIRST Championship, where they are edged out in the division finals by a heavily favored rival.

On a honeymoon trip to Tunis with his new wife, the Parisian scholar Michel is struck by tuberculosis. As he recuperates, he rediscovers the joys of living and decides to abandon his past scholarly pursuits in order to seize the present—wanting the layers of learned knowledge to peel away from his mind like a cosmetic, revealing in patches the naked flesh beneath and the authentic self concealed there. Yet this is not the Michel his colleagues recognize, nor the Michel who will be readily accepted by conventional society, and he must mask his newly formed values beneath a veneer of the very attitudes he now despises. Disenchanted with Parisian society, he relocates to a family farm in Normandy, finding happiness there, especially in the company of the young Charles. Nevertheless, he soon returns to the city and to academic life. Michel remains unsettled until his first lecture, where he encounters Ménalque—a longtime provocateur of society who perceives in Michel a kindred torment. He then drifts further south, into the desert, until, as he tells his friends, he becomes lost in a sea of sand. Gide’s tale is rich with prose that vividly renders Michel’s outward voyage and his inner terrain: the African earth, awake after months of immersion, overflowing with water and new sap, laughing in a springtime frenzy whose echo he also senses within himself.

A mysterious woman in black pursues Chinese Cinderella, and the tale opens with CC fleeing. After a fall, she ends up in hospital, where she overhears a famed painting, Along The River at Qing Ming, referenced in the ward. Suffering sudden, unpredictable blackouts, CC is tormented by dreams—vivid, strange, yet oddly familiar. An adventure unfolds, weaving threads of friendship, wealth and poverty, eunuchs, and an emperor who adored art. The narrative transports CC eight centuries back, to the Song Dynasty, as she drifts between wakefulness and slumber. Following another collapse, she is carried to medical care once more. As her consciousness ebbs and flows, these dreams persist, haunting her with their uncanny resonance. Thus begins CC’s emotional voyage back to a life of privilege imagined from a distant era. In her present, she is the daughter of a powerful, prosperous man, yet she finds herself drawn to a poor orphan boy who possesses a remarkable gift for capturing nature’s beauty. As their bond grows, art and tender love begin to clash with the stubborn, stratified codes of Chinese society.

The story begins in Santa Barbara, California. Travis Cornell, a former Delta Force operative, feels that his life has grown pointless, and is exploring a canyon near his home when he encounters two genetically engineered creatures that have escaped from a top-secret government lab. One, a golden retriever with extraordinarily enhanced intelligence, befriends Travis; the other, a terrifying creature known as the Outsider, appears to be trying to kill the dog. After eluding the Outsider, Travis takes the dog home and names him Einstein. Meanwhile, Nora Devon, an introverted young woman, whose abusive aunt recently has died, is attacked in her home by a man who attempts to rape her. Travis and Einstein intervene and the three quickly form a tight bond. Travis, Nora, and Einstein soon find themselves on the run not only from the Outsider, but from federal agents determined to track down the lab escapees, and Vince Nasco, a ruthless professional assassin, hired to kill the creatures and eliminate any witnesses he may encounter along the way.

From the hardcover jacket: An invasion of rabbits seems inevitable for Australia. Millions of creatures, now immune to the myxomatosis that had devastated them in the mid-20th century, flood the countryside. With an election looming, Prime Minister Kevin Fitzgerald—nickname Ella among his circle—must take action. The situation is framed as an emergency: the rabbits must be eradicated. Scientists mobilize and experiments commence. The outcomes are catastrophic. Suddenly Australia dominates as the planet’s most formidable power: in rapid succession, America, Russia, and the other major powers hand over their nuclear arsenals; Fitzgerald effectively governs the world. The Commonwealth Government, in an effort to secure lasting peace, enacts a global order in which only limited wars are permitted and conducted under strict Canberra-approved rules. Only two nations may engage in combat at a time, for instance. Yet, as this remarkable era of prosperity surges forward, a minor news brief slips through unnoticed: a rabbit—massive, as large as an Alsatian—shot by a Sunday-school teacher three miles north of Mudgee.

Odysseus leaves Ithaca once more, seeking fresh exploits after quickly tiring of domestic life. His first halt is Sparta, where he aims to rescue Helen, wife of Menelaus, whose abduction by Paris sparked the Trojan War. From there he proceeds to Crete, where a coup dethrones the king, and he abandons Helen along the way. His journey then carries him to Egypt, where another workers’ uprising erupts. He continues onward along the Nile, eventually reaching the lake-source, and there his companions erect camp while he ascends a mountain to commune with his god. Returning to the lake, he establishes a city guided by his religious commandments. An earthquake soon razes this settlement, and Odysseus mourns his failure to grasp the true divine meaning, sacrificing his companions in the process. His life shifts into asceticism. Along his path, he encounters Motherth, a figure representing the Buddha; Kapetan Enas, known in English as Captain Sole and, alias Don Quixote; and a fisherman from an African village who is identified with Jesus. He travels deeper into Africa, continually spreading his faith and resisting death’s advances. In time he reaches Antarctica, living for a year among villagers before an iceberg ends his life. His death is celebrated as glorious, signaling his rebirth and unity with the world.”

The protagonist is a fifteen year old African American boy named Bobby who lives in an apartment in South Bronx with his mother and siblings. Despite his young age Bobby has intelligence that is advanced to most of the people around him. Bobby's Hispanic girlfriend Maria often spend time together and have plans for the upcoming summer. Bobby and Maria's lives are shattered when a vicious Hispanic street gang attack Bobby and Maria while the two were walking to school. Bobby and Maria are severely beaten and Maria is sent to the hospital suffering from near-fatal wounds. After Bobby is beaten he gets picked up by an old holocaust survivor named Moishe and an unlikely friendship between Bobby and Moishe begins. Maria, unable to cope with the mutilation of her face caused by the lye, commits suicide. We hear Moishe talking about his tragic story while he was in a concentration camp, while Bobby tells Moishe what has happened to him and Maria. Bobby states that deep in his mind, he still has a desperate need for revenge.

After Starfleet unveils a new android, its destruction sparks Lieutenant Commander Data’s investigation into the culprit. In the process, Data uncovers a truth: he may not be as solitary as he once believed. Throughout the original Star Trek series, audiences saw numerous robots and androids, yet Data is frequently portrayed as the sole android roaming the era of Star Trek: The Next Generation. Immortal Coil clarifies the fate of those other artificial beings and clarifies how Data’s story intertwines with theirs. The narrative nods to several previously introduced intelligences and characters, including: Exocomps from The Next Generation episode The Quality of Life; the androids from The Original Series episode What Are Little Girls Made Of?; the M5 computer from The Original Series episode The Ultimate Computer; Flint and Reyna from The Original Series episode Requiem for Methuselah; Doctor Ira Graves from The Next Generation episode The Schizoid Man; Commander Bruce Maddox from The Next Generation episode The Measure of a Man; and Dr. Noonien Soong, Data’s creator, first encountered in The Next Generation episode Brothers.

After having haughtily refused a number of suitors, under the pretext that they are not peers of France, Émilie de Fontaine falls in love with a mysterious young man who quietly appeared at the village dance at Sceaux. Despite his refined appearance and aristocratic bearing, the unknown (Maximilien Longueville) never tells his identity and seems interested in nobody but his sister, a sickly young girl. But he is not insensible to the attention Émilie gives him and he accepts the invitation of Émilie’s father, the Comte de Fontaine. Émilie and Maximilien soon fall in love. The Comte de Fontaine, concerned for his daughter, decides to investigate this mysterious young man, and he discovers him on the Rue du Sentier, a simple cloth merchant, which horrifies Émilie. Piqued, she marries a 70 year old uncle for his title of Vice Admiral, the Comte de Kergarouët. Several years after her marriage, Émilie discovers that Maximilien is not a clothier at all, but in fact a Vicomte de Longueville who has become a Peer of France. The young man finally explains why he secretly tended a store: he did it in order to support his family, sacrificing himself for his sick sister and for his brother, who had departed the country.

Dr. Roseveare, the headmaster of the relatively obscure English public school at Oakington, has spent seven years striving to elevate its standing. In the winter term of 1927–1928, a pupil dies in his sleep when an old gas fitting collapses from the ceiling, prompting Roseveare to enlist Colin Revell, an alumnus, to conduct a discreet inquiry. Although Revell harbors reservations about ruling out foul play, he cannot identify a clear motive, so he departs after a few weeks, and the investigation’s trail is largely erased by the building’s conversion to electricity. A few months later, Revell is startled by news that the dead boy’s brother, also an orphaned survivor, has perished under enigmatic circumstances—apparently leaping into the school’s indoor pool after the water had been drained—and he travels to Oakington of his own accord. There, he discovers that the brothers’ closest surviving relative is a teacher at the school, and that this teacher stands to inherit a modest fortune. Simultaneously, Revell finds himself falling in love with the teacher’s stunning young wife.

Set in 18th‑century Japan, the tale centers on a quartet of distinctly different figures whose paths cross around Matari, a woman whose allure draws three men who each fall in love with her in their own way. Oboko, a wind‑loving poet and Buddhist monk (the name hints at Zen such as Obaku), Izzi, an outgoing court poet, Lord Arishi, a samurai and ruler, and Matari herself—beautiful, clever, and fleeing for her life—form the core ensemble. Although the narrative might be read as a love story, the protagonists’ divergent views on life, honor, and morality set up a fatal clash when their loyalties converge. The novel adheres to a comparatively traditional structure, unfolding linearly with a plot you could find in many books, yet Cockcroft’s deft incorporation of Zen philosophy provides a thoughtful, well‑rounded glimpse into Buddhist and samurai mindsets. Oboko survives the events and is later referenced in The Book of the Die, another work by the same author. The book has appeared in several editions under varying ISBNs: 0-246-10811-8 (Matari, hardcover, January 1975); 0-586-04116-8 (Matari, paperback, September 2, 1976); 1-4033-4796-4 (White Wind, Black Rider, hardcover, November 27, 2002); 1-4033-4795-6 (White Wind, Black Rider, paperback, November 27, 2002).

Camilla is facing significant problems at home. Her mother, Rose, has begun an affair with a man named Jacques. Her mother begs Camilla to keep it a secret, while Camilla's father, Rafferty, asks her to be honest and tell him the truth. Camilla is torn between her loyalty to both parents and begins to realize they are very imperfect people. To cope with the struggle, Camilla befriends Frank, her best friend's older brother. He is understanding of her problems and assists her in accepting her parents flaws. Frank encourages Camilla to define herself not by her family but to define herself as who she truly is. The pair share ideas on life, religion and philosophy and begin to form a romantic attachment. Their happiness is cut short when their families problems get worse. Frank's parents break up and he is forced to suddenly move away with his father. Camilla's parents decide to work on their marriage and go on a European Vacation together. Unfortunately, while her parents are traveling, Camilla is going to be sent to a Swiss boarding school. While Camilla is heartbroken by the loss of Frank, she uses the inner strength she has gained in the past weeks to deal with the changes in her life.

The novel opens as an experimental star ship tests a deadly weapon on an uninhabited world, devastating the surface. From here the story essentially follows the two main characters as they are recruited by the Sutherlin Alliance in their bid to overthrow the Alcon Empire. The junior of the two opens the story as a pilot in the Empire’s prestigious Devil Squadron. The senior recruit had also once served in this fighter group only to resign years early and take up the life of a mercenary and bounty hunter. With these two skilled men added to their backbone of ex-Imperial soldiers and raw youth from around the galaxy the Alliance takes the fight to the Empire. With the threat of the Alliance growing the Empire learns of their location and decides to unleash the power of their world killing star ship. The two recruited men learn of the ship’s existence and its target just days before its use and develop a plan of attack to cripple both the ship and the sizable force escorting it. One of the themes that is expressed throughout the story is attachment and the human need to belong; both main characters fight with these needs in their own ways. The elder of the two battles the desire with his own wishes to stay separate from the needs of the others while the younger fights to keep his distance, not wanting to feel the loss of war.

One day in the Cretaceous Period as a Tyrannosaurus is about to devour a smaller dino he captured, a flying saucer piloted by an alien named Vorb arrives. He recruits him and several other dinos he's found for a trial of a special "vitamin" he's developed, which, upon feeding it to the dinos, causes them to become sapient. Vorb takes them aboard his saucer and they travel to the present, dropping them off in New York City, which at that moment is celebrating the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. The dinos pretend to be inflatable balloons to sneak along with the parade, but Rex mistakes one of the real dino balloons to be his friend Allosaurus. The ruse is broken as a result of him accidentally popping "Allosaurus" and the dinos flee as the crowd panics in sight of them. The police come to capture the dinos soon after, but the helpful curator of the American Museum of Natural History, Dr. Bleeb, takes the dinos in, and hides them from the cops by having them pretend to be life-size model dinosaurs. This satisfies the police, who leave to search for the dinosaurs elsewhere, and the curator lets them stay for the night. She reads them a bedtime story about a trilobite who wanted to walk on land, while the dinos watch out the window, unsure about their future. ru:Мы вернулись! История динозавра

In 2010 Denver, a man named Thomas Hunter experiences a head wound from a gunshot that leaves him unconscious. When he awakens, he finds himself amid a bizarre landscape of black, twisted trees. After being attacked by bat-like beings called Shataiki, and then led out of the Black Forest by a white bat, he inexplicably slips back into unconsciousness from blood loss and later wakes again in Denver. He is startled by the abrupt shift and cannot determine which world is real. Soon he realizes a troubling pattern: every time he drifts to sleep, he regresses to the other realm, and only returns when he dozes there again. Beyond the Black Forest lies the Colored Forest, a utopian region inhabited by immortal yet innocent humans and overseen by Elyon, a god-like figure. Roush, pure white and bat-like, accompanies Elyon as a servant, acting as a foil to the Shataiki. Thomas uncovers the shocking truth that the alternate world is actually our future, thousands of years ahead, and that a virus—deriving from a mutated vaccine—will devastate his present-day Earth later that same year. He is compelled to confront evil across both realities, a daunting task since each realm depicts malevolence differently, yet both are equally formidable. Ultimately, stopping a catastrophic event proves to be an arduous challenge for him.

A second Raman vessel enters our solar system seventy years after Rendezvous with Rama. Its arrival is anticipated, and a mission is dispatched to uncover more of Rama’s secrets, yet the crew confronts unforeseen discoveries and internal conflicts. Rama II introduces new characters into a fresh narrative that largely stands apart from the first work and mainly serves to lay groundwork for its own sequels. The tale concludes with three of the twelve astronauts—Nicole des Jardins Wakefield, Richard Wakefield, and Michael O’Toole—left stranded inside Rama as it drifts beyond the solar system. In contrast to Rendezvous with Rama, which portrayed a utopian future and concentrated on hard-science marvels of the alien craft, Rama II and its successors undermine Clarke’s optimistic view of solar-system colonization by depicting a global economic collapse that nearly extinguishes human activity. The series then pivots to a markedly different storytelling approach, foregrounding contemporary issues such as abortion, racism, drug abuse, and organized crime.

The plot concerns four college students who discover a manuscript, The Book of Skulls, dealing with an order of monks living in a monastery in the Arizona desert, whose members have the power to bestow immortality on those who complete their bizarre initiation rite. The boys travel to the monastery, where they are accepted as a "Receptacle," and told that for each group of four who agree to undergo the ritual, two must die in order for the others to succeed - one must sacrifice himself, and the other must be sacrificed. The narrative switches back and forth between the viewpoints of the four students as each confronts his personal demons on the way to completing the ritual. Ned, who is openly homosexual, must face his guilt over the tragic aftermath of one of his affairs; Eli, the gifted (but socially inept) young man who discovered the manuscript, makes a confession that could destroy his academic career; Timothy, star athlete and prodigal son of a wealthy family, confronts a terrible sin from his past involving his younger sister; and Oliver, the farm kid from the wrong side of the tracks, comes face to face with his own true innermost nature. The Book of Skulls has been republished as part of the series SF Masterworks.

The narrative begins in 2021, inside a nation ruled by a tyrant named Jeeva. His regime enforces population control: aging citizens are allowed to live only up to a fixed age and are killed once they surpass it. Every person must bear a government-assigned two-letter name, and all citizens are compelled to follow Jeeva’s dictates while publicly worshiping him. A vast network of robots pervades society, and identities are reduced to social security numbers stored and managed by a master computer in the capital. On New Year’s Eve, Nila, a homemaker, celebrates receiving government approval to bear a son from the Population Control Board. She shares the news with her husband, Sibi. Meanwhile, the state designates Nila’s home for a man named Ravi and his robotic pet, Jeano. Government rules cap the number of occupants at three, so Sibi leaves to confirm Ravi’s allotment but never returns. Desperate, Nila searches for him using his social security number, only to discover that no such person exists. Frustrated and fearful, she continues the search without success. What happened to Sibi? What role does Ravi play in his disappearance? How will Nila uncover the truth about Jeeva’s dictatorship with Jeano’s help? The remainder of the story unravels as these questions are answered.

Julian, Dick and Anne arrive in Cornwall to stay with George for the holidays. They plan to spend time exploring Kirrin Island but their happiness is spoilt when Aunt Fanny falls ill and has to leave with Uncle Quentin to be treated in a far-off hospital. They are cared for by Aunt Fanny's temporary cook, Mrs Stick, who is accompanied by her husband and their ghastly son Edgar. The Sticks and the children come to hate each other. When Mrs Stick tries to poison George's dog Timmy, George can take it no more. She hatches a secret plan to run away to Kirrin island and look after herself but when Julian catches her leaving she decides to allow the other children to go with her. While on the island, they find evidence of smugglers on an old wreck. A scream in the night and the discovery of a young girl's clothes alert the Five that there could be something very sinister going on. They discover that the Sticks have kidnapped and imprisoned a little girl on the island, the daughter of a very rich man. Having tormented the Sticks into a retreat they rescue the girl, taking her to the police who are amazed to see the child "the whole country is looking for!!" The police accompany them back to the island in time to trap and arrest the Sticks. The kidnapped girl's father allows her to spend a week with her new friends on Kirrin Island.

The text surveys a range of threats—environmental degradation, famine, overpopulation, climate shifts, floods, tornadoes, and the hothouse/greenhouse effect among them—and projects them as intensifying toward the end of the 20th century. Berlitz compiles an extensive roster of predicted doomsdays, beginning with December 31, 999, when many anticipated Christ’s return, and continuing through numerous forecasts by scientists, prophets, astrologers, and other voices. In chapter 8, he questions whether the world has ever truly ended, invoking Atlantis as an example—a notion he revisits later in The Mystery of Atlantis and Atlantis: The Lost Continent Revealed. He entertains the possibility that a flood may have occurred, a theory he examines further in The Lost Ship of Noah: In Search of the Ark at Ararat (1987). In chapter 9, he cites flood legends from the Bible and the Torah, alongside accounts from Sumerian, Babylonian, Assyrian, Greek, Indian, Persian, Welsh, Norse, Lithuanian, Irish, Chinese, Aztec-Toltec, Mayan, and Chibcha sources."

The Shepherd’s Paradise presents a mythical pastoral realm devoted to Platonic affection, serving as a sanctuary for unrequited lovers of both sexes—a tranquil haven for troubled minds. Its ruler is Bellesa, symbolizing beauty, who was almost certainly portrayed by Henrietta Maria. Fidamira is the play’s central heroine. Much of Montagu’s plot revolves around Basilino, a prince, and his close companion Agenor, who share a tendency to fall for the same women. The drama complicates itself with disguise: Basilino operates under the name Moramente, while Agenor assumes Genorio. By the play’s end, Agenor/Genorio is unmasked as Prince Palante, the Navarre king’s long-lost son. A prominent masque within also hosts a lengthy inquiry into the essence of love, featuring Martiro advocating the Platonic ideal, contrasted with Moramente and Melidoro who defend marriage. The finale aligns with conventional comic marriages: Basilino, now Moramente, weds Bellesa—who is in fact Sapphira, Princess of Navarre and his original betrothed—while Agenor/Genorio/Palante weds Basilino’s sister. This ending invites readings that celebrate marital union over Platonic affection. Fidamira is revealed to be sister to both Bellesa/Sapphira and Agenor/Genorio/Palante, the lost Miranda, remaining a virgin yet attaining queenship of the Shepherd’s Paradise in the conclusion.

Fresh from the Bacta War on Thyferra, Wedge Antilles sets his sights on forming a new fighter squadron—this time a hybrid of combat commandos with pilots as a secondary consideration. While presenting the plan to Admiral Ackbar, he outlines a cost-free approach for the New Republic: recruit the misfits, the washouts, and those pilots barely clinging to Fighter Command status—those no one else will take. In contrast to Rogue Squadron, built from elite pilots who also had ground-fighting chops, this unit would consist of seasoned ground fighters whose piloting ability would be secondary. With Wes Janson's aid, Antilles assembles a crew that becomes known as Wraith Squadron, featuring: Jesmin Ackbar, a communications specialist and Admiral Ackbar’s niece; Hohass “Runt” Ekwesh, a Thakwaash with multiple personalities; Garik “Face” Loran, once a child actor recruited by the Empire; Voort “Piggy” SaBinring, a Gamorrean who pilots; Kell Tainer, a demolitions expert and the son of a Rebel pilot Antilles was forced to kill; Myn Donos, the sole survivor of an Imperial ambush against his Talon squadron; Ton Phanan, a former doctor with some mechanical augmentation; Falynn Sandskimmer, a Tatooine vehicle expert known for insolence; Tyria Sarkin, a former Antari Ranger with minor Force sensitivity; and Eurrsk “Grinder” Thri’ag, an accomplished code slicer and prankster. The story centers on Wraith Squadron’s misadventures as they go undercover aboard Night Caller, an Imperial blockade runner hired by Warlord Zsinj, to accompany the crew on a covert mission.

In The Forests of Silence, the topaz had been retrieved by Lief, Barda, and Jasmine. They continue on their way to the Lake of Tears, to retrieve the ruby. They learn that the land surrounding the Lake of Tears is controlled by the evil sorceress Thaegan, who has 13 monster children. As the companions travel through the countryside they rescue a man named Manus from the Shadow Lord's servants, Grey Guards. Manus is from the city of Raladin. 100 years ago, Thaegan put a spell on Raladin that caused them and all of their offspring to never be able to speak. Lief, Barda, and Jasmine also learn that Thaegan put a spell on the city of D'Or and turned it into the Lake of Tears. The companions, with Manus, escape from the Grey Guards only to be captured by Jin and Jod, two of Thaegan's children. They eventually defeat Jin and Jod and journey to the city of Raladin, where Manus hopes to find his people. Upon arrival, they find the city empty. Only when the Ralad people hear the companions, they come out of hiding. Lief, Barda, and Jasmine tell the Ralads that they must journey to the Lake of Tears, despite the Ralads pleas, but they do not tell them they are going in quest of one of the gems of the Belt of Deltora. Manus agrees to be their guide. When they get to the Lake of Tears, the monster Soldeen attacks them. Soldeen is a giant fish-like creature who is very deadly and has the ability to speak. Using the power of the topaz, Lief persuades Soldeen to give them the ruby. As Soldeen agrees, Thaegan appears and threatens to kill them all. The ruby flies out of Lief's hand and into the depths of the Lake as Thaegan uses her magic to harm them. Just as Thaegan is about to kill them all, Jasmine's bird Kree comes and kills Thaegan by drawing blood. All of Thaegan's spells are broken: the Ralads can now speak and the Lake of Tears turns back into the city of D'Or. Soldeen is a man named Nanion and gives the three companions the gem and wishes them well on their quest. The Belt now holds the topaz and ruby and now they journey towards the City of the Rats.

Detective Chief Inspector Alan Banks’s career has lately seemed stalled, nearly ruined by the petty squabbles of his politically driven superior, Chief Constable Riddle. The turning point comes when nude images of Riddle’s runaway teenage daughter appear on a porn site, forcing Riddle to seek Banks’s aid. Banks traces the trail first to Soho in London—an enclave of strip clubs and sex shops—and then to the refined district of Little Venice, where Emily Riddle resides with a dangerous gangster connected to the rock world. Initially, Emily resists returning home, but she later reappears at Banks’s hotel, battered and frightened, pleading for help. She eventually goes back to her family in Yorkshire, and Banks believes his involvement is finished. Yet other matters demand his attention. Eastvale Regional Headquarters undergoes a sweeping reorganization and expansion, bringing Detective Sergeant Annie Cabbot back into Banks’s orbit, where she confronts her own inner struggles. As they start investigating the murder of Charlie Courage, a petty criminal, a new homicide erupts at an Eastvale nightclub, fueling tabloid headlines about scandal, sex, and high-level corruption. The brutal killing deeply unsettles Banks and eventually unveils connections that tie it to the Charlie Courage case. The investigation’s grim findings push Banks toward an unwanted path, forcing him to confront the past and the private life of his most formidable adversary, Chief Constable Riddle.

Amanda McCready disappeared from a Boston neighborhood in 1997 when she was just four. Desperate appeals from her aunt drew in the shrewd, stubborn sleuths Patrick Kenzie and Angie Gennaro, who took on the case with everything at stake. They chased her down only to arrange her return to a neglectful mother and a fractured home. Now, at sixteen, Amanda is gone again. An exceptional student, bright yet distant, she seemed fated to break free from her upbringing. Her aunt returns to Kenzie’s door, worried about the girl who has blossomed into a striking, intelligent young woman and has vanished for two weeks. Carrying the weight of the past, Kenzie and Gennaro reopen the case that haunted them most, tracing a twelve-year web of secrets and lies through Boston’s rough, blue-collar streets. They persuade themselves that this time will be different, determined to locate Amanda and ensure her safety. Yet their resolve to do the right thing carries dark stakes—stakes that could claim Amanda’s life and their own. In the interval since Prayers for Rain, Kenzie and Gennaro have married and started a family.

Ten-year-old Liza Barton accidentally killed her mother and wounded her stepfather, Ted. Though acquitted, she is later adopted by distant relatives. Fast-forward twenty-four years, Liza—now living as Celia Foster—strives to erase her past and begins a new life with Alex Nolan, following the death of her first husband, Larry. Unbeknownst to Alex, Celia’s history runs deeper. He gifts her a birthday surprise: the keys to her own parents’ house in the neighboring town of Mendham. The threesome—Celia, Alex, and their four-year-old son, Jack—move in only to discover the home has been vandalized. To avoid upsetting Alex, Celia decides to conceal her history for the time being. Memories of the fatal night flood Celia’s mind as she starts to uncover the truth about what happened that evening. She also quietly seeks information about the accident that claimed her father’s life a year before her mother’s death. As several elderly townspeople are murdered one by one, clues increasingly point toward Celia. With the killer’s pursuit accelerating, Celia’s own life becomes imperiled while the mystery of her past closes in.

La Vendetta is a short work relating the tragic fate of Ginevra Piombo, the daughter of proud Corsican immigrants, who has the misfortune of falling in love with another Corsican Luigi Porta. When it becomes known that Luigi is the sole survivor of a massacre in which the rest of his family were the victims of a bloody vendetta with Ginevra's family, Ginevra's father Bartolomeo is determined to complete the act of vengeance by having him killed. But Ginevra refuses to yield to her father's demands and she and Luigi are married. Over the following years the pair eke out a miserable existence, dogged by hunger and poverty, while Ginevra's wealthy father refuses to lift a hand to support her: it is as much as he can do to refrain from murdering Luigi. Ginevra gives birth to a child, but she and the child die on the very day that Monsieur Piombo finally relents and decides to assist the impoverished couple. Before he can act, however, Luigi visits him and gives him the tresses of his deceased daughter. "Dead! Our two families were doomed to exterminate each other. Here is all that remains of her," he says, laying Ginevra's long black hair upon the table. Ginevra's parents are shaken, as though a stroke of lightning has blasted them. Luigi departs. "He has spared me a shot, for he is dead," says Bartolomeo, slowly, gazing on the ground at his feet.

Eric Packer, a 28-year-old billionaire asset manager, grinds a peculiar odyssey through midtown Manhattan to reach a haircut. His stretch limo, described in exquisite detail as luxurious, expansive, and technologically equipped, glides with blocked-out street noise courtesy of cork lining, bulletproofing, Carrara marble floors, and a wall of television screens and computer monitors. Packer’s progress is repeatedly impeded by a presidential visit, a vociferous anti-capitalist riot, and a funeral procession for a Sufi rap star. Along this journey, he has several chance exchanges with his wife and engages in extramarital affairs. He is tailed by two men: a comically inept “pastry assassin” and a volatile, self-styled “credible threat.” As the day unfolds, Packer watches enormous sums vanish from his clients’ accounts due to bets against the yen’s ascent, a loss that mirrors his own financial and personal unraveling. He appears to take grim pleasure in relinquishing wealth, even ensuring his wife’s fortune is squandered to seal his ruin. In the end, the second stalker—a former employee who views Packer’s murder as the only meaningful act left—shoots him to death.

When Nita's sister Dairine signs up for an intragalactic exchange program without permission, their local advisors transfer the mission to Nita and Kit. The destination seems to be an ideal planet, and they are hoping for a vacation. Meanwhile, the aliens who arrive at Dairine's house appear to be very "alien". However, Nita's dreams become nightmarish and the planet Alaalu turns out to be hiding a dark secret: an avatar of the Lone Power has been trapped in this dystopia since their people refused Its gift of entropy. While this may have prevented deterioration to war, crime and natural disasters, among other things, it also prevented such change as evolution, and the Alaalu people are trapped in their current stage of existence when they have the potential to be free of it. It becomes the young wizards' job to convince the Alaalu wizard and her people to accept this change, inevitably setting the Lone Power free. On Earth, the wizards at Dairine's place have become aware that their Sun is in danger of flaring up to the point of scorching their planet. However, one of the visitors comes from a planet where he is a guardian against the recurrence of such a disaster, and recognizes it in time for them to save the Earth.

Chelsea’s family resolution keeps her from hosting a birthday party because of the expected cost. Meanwhile, her envy grows as Geneva and Warwick, her siblings, receive more money from their parents. In the Stomping Ground nightclub, she forms a friendship with Bex, which deepens a few weeks later after Fee’s friend Eddie tries to assault Chelsea; Bex intervenes to protect her. Separately, Barry Gee launches his own restaurant venture, christening it Gee Zone. Jemma longs to pursue acting, but her parents object when she sacrifices schoolwork for acting and dancing lessons. She disregards their concerns, placing faith in Ms. Olivia Ockley, the owner of the acting school, who praises her abilities. Friction arises, however, when Alexa Browning lands a lead role ahead of Jemma. Jemma’s romance with Rob strains her bond with Chelsea, though they repair their relationship following Chelsea’s confrontation with Eddie. Jon begins to like Sumitha, but she has lost interest. He is also irritated by his busy parents. After Laura is injured during one of his mother’s animal-rights demonstrations, he realizes his feelings for her and asks her out. Laura’s mother is pregnant, while her boyfriend Melvyn resents Laura’s participation in demonstrations with her neighbor Daniel. Laura’s brother arrives prematurely, and, at Laura’s suggestion, is named Charlie. Sumitha turns into a diligent student—an admirer of her new science teacher, Paul Sharpe—yet, at term’s end, she reveals her crush only to learn that Paul is engaged to Mrs. McConnell. When Sandeep asks her to return home with him, Sumitha dismisses him, and later feels remorse upon discovering that he is being bullied by Kevin and Matthew.

The Maasai people become aware that a global crisis is approaching. Malevolent, unearthly creatures called shetani, which inhabit another dimension the Maasai know as the “Out Of” (because all things, such as humans, animals and plants, originally came "out of" it), are finding their way into the world. They are fomenting trouble between the superpowers, intent on causing mischief up to and including war. If not prevented, the barriers between the two dimensions will be breached and uncountable hordes of shetani will overrun the world, destroying all life. Olkeloki, a Maasai elder, comes to Washington DC to warn the US President and seek help. He encounters Joshua Oak, a disenchanted FBI agent, and Merry Sharrow, a shy and unfulfilled call centre worker. He is convinced that they are the key people he has been seeking, and his persuasion, coupled with several dangerous encounters with shetani, convince them to return with him to Africa, where they join in Maasai attempts to hold back the shetani. Eventually Olkeloki takes Merry and Oak into the Out Of, where, with their help, he performs a ritual which seals the breach between dimensions, sacrificing his own supernatural powers in the process. All three return to this world, where the shetani’s tricks have ended and the diplomatic crisis is receding, and Oak and Merry realise they have found what they have been looking for in each other.

In Baltimore’s predominantly Eastern European enclave, December 1941 frames the meeting of Michael Anton and Pauline Barclay as he tends to her bloodied brow in his family’s grocery store. Their bond leads to marriage after Michael leaves the Army with a permanent injury inflicted by a deliberate shot from a man he had attacked. The couple sets up residence in a small flat above the shop, yet their starkly contrasting temperaments—his repressed, controlling, and reticent nature versus her loud, emotional, and romantic disposition—soon sow discord. At Pauline’s urging, they relocate to the suburbs and raise three children: Lindy, George, and Karen. Lindy flees to San Francisco in 1960, drawn into the emergent drug scene. Eight years afterward, her parents reclaim Pagan, their three-year-old grandchild, as Lindy undergoes rehabilitation. The marriage gradually unravels, culminating in Michael abandoning Pauline on their thirtieth anniversary. For him, the sense that they were utterly unprepared for marriage, “amateurs” in the domestic domain, makes divorce a form of salvation; for Pauline, it becomes a tragedy that leaves her engulfed in despair.
